James’ The Children of Men is yet another very British book, but the parts of the story that fascinated Cuarón weren’t about the people who rise to power or gather to argue about the world’s problems, or even the details of how the near-future world functions. He was looking at it from post-9/11 perspective on world politics and thinking about how he could employ a more intimate scope to use the movie’s speculative world to illuminate our real one.
To do that, he narrowed the scope of the story compared to what’s in the novel, and shifted the sociopolitical commentary away from exploring how and why authoritarian regimes rise to power, moving instead toward looking at what the societies they build do to the least powerful among them. The speculative element underlying the near-future world is more or less the same: Nearly two decades ago, humanity suffered a mass infertility epidemic that science has not been able to cure, and no children have been born since. Cuarón has said repeatedly (probably because he was asked repeatedly) that he had absolutely no interest in trying to explain the infertility, because as soon as you start explaining it people start nitpicking the explanation. He’s completely right about that. He’s also right that it’s irrelevant.
The film follows Theo Faron (Clive Owen), a man living in London in the futuristic year of 2027. Very little about the world is exposited directly, but we learn enough to know that many terrible things have befallen cities and nations around the world. The United Kingdom has closed its borders to immigration and showers the population with propaganda about how Britain is the last civilized place in the world. Refugees are violently rounded up, locked into cages, and shipped to internment camps.
…I know. This won’t be the last time we all collectively pause to stare dully into the middle distance and think about how this movie came out in 2006 and has only become more resonant over the past twenty years.
Theo is an interesting character for a movie that ends up having quite a lot of action in it. While the film is tightly confined to his perspective, he’s not actually a very active protagonist, at least not at first. He’s deeply depressed but not numb, although it seems like he wishes he could be; the only warmth and connection in his life is the time he spends with his hippie friend Jasper (Michael Caine cosplaying as John Lennon). When a group of pro-immigration activists led by Theo’s ex, Julian (Julianne Moore), abduct him and demand that he help them, he at first refuses, then reluctantly agrees to do it for the money, not the ideology. Julian’s group wants papers to help transport an undocumented young woman, Kee (Clare-Hope Ashitey), safely to some unknown destination.
After Julian is killed in an ambush, Theo learns that Kee is pregnant—the world’s first known pregnancy in eighteen years. Julian had been helping her escape Britain to meet up with a group of people trying to solve humanity’s infertility. But Julian’s successor, Luke (Chiwetel Ejiofor), wants to use Kee and her child to persuade the British government to change its policies, so Theo, Kee, and another woman, Miriam (Pam Ferris) flee the group to make it to Kee’s rendezvous and get her out of the country.
From the ambush and Julian’s death all the way to the end, Children of Men is a chase movie. It is all about getting from one place to another while evading people who want to stop them. I don’t think this is a bad thing. In fact, I think it’s great. Many excellent movies are chase movies! The Terminator (1984) is a chase movie. Alfred Hitchcock’s North by Northwest (1959) is a chase movie. One of the greatest movies ever made (according to me), George Miller’s Mad Max: Fury Road (2015), is the purest distillation of a chase movie.
Of course, a chase isn’t engaging if we don’t care about who’s being chased and why, and we won’t care about those things if the concentrated action feels disconnected from larger stakes or consequences. An interesting thing about Children of Men is how the movie manages this by being very careful in what it doesn’t tell us. We know that Kee and her child are important, not just because protecting a mother and newborn is always important, but because the world will change with them in it. But we don’t know how. We don’t know what will become of Kee when she reaches the rendezvous. We can’t know, because Theo and Kee don’t know, and the film never strays from its tight focus on them. We don’t even really know who Kee is going to meet. Just like the characters, we’re asked to trust that she is running in the right direction, and that Theo is doing the right thing by helping her.
Without knowing what the endpoint is going to be, the film has to prove to us that it probably won’t be worse than where the characters start. And that’s not enough. The chase itself also has to be interesting.
It helps that the cast is fantastic—Owen and Ashitey are wonderful as two characters who would otherwise have absolutely no reason to interact—and the danger escalates relentlessly without ever feeling like we’re losing track of what’s going on.
Even beyond that, there are two specific achievements of the production that elevate Children of Men from ‘pretty good dystopian action movie’ to a truly great film. The first is the efficiency of the worldbuilding, and the second is the astonishing craftsmanship that went into the cinematography and visual effects.
In a 2006 article, Cuarón explained how he modeled his approach to Children of Men on the Italian-Algerian war film The Battle of Algiers (1966), directed by Gillo Pontecorvo. The Battle of Algiers is a movie about Algerian revolutionaries during the war for independence from France in the ’50s; it’s a fictionalized reconstruction based on the tactics and events of the campaign, but it’s filmed in the style of a newsreel or documentary, with a cast made up of non-professional actors, to mimic the feeling of watching real-world events play out on television news. Cuarón said of the film, “The amazing thing about The Battle of Algiers is the social reconstruction. It’s meticulous, and the sense of reality is so unique.”
The speculative premise behind Children of Men is introduced in the opening scene, where Theo and the world learn about the senseless death of the world’s youngest person. The nature of the world is revealed moments later, when the coffee shop Theo has just exited is destroyed by a bomb—and he still goes to work. When he decides to cut out early, it’s the death of an eighteen-year-old across the world that he uses as an excuse for his boss, not the fact that he was steps away from being blown to pieces in a senseless act of violence. Along the way we see news reports, propaganda, advertisements for gentle suicide drugs, and armed soldiers keeping people in cages at train stations, and it’s all vivid and visceral enough that was we can feel how miserable and unsafe it would be to walk those streets. We understand why Theo is depressed, why Jasper hides in the woods to grow and smoke weed, why the dissidents lash out with so much anger, why strangers weep over the death of a teenager they’ve never met.
The movie was filmed on location in London in 2005, which means they were creating a fake terrorist bombing mere weeks after real terrorist bombings in the city. But London of 2005 didn’t look like the dystopian London of 2027 the film needed, so Cuarón brought on visual effects supervisor Frazer Churchill to transport the extremely familiar sights—Fleet Street, Trafalgar Square, Battersea Power Station—into a grimier, grittier future, one where many people have given up on the hope of things ever getting better. It was an even bigger task to transform the real town of Bexhill-on-Sea into the crumbling, overcrowded refugee internment camp without any of it looking fake or computer-generated.
And amidst all that, there is, of course, a newborn baby, who is an on-set dummy covered by CGI, because a premature VFX newborn preserves our immersion in the story better than a real, clean, chubby baby of the wrong age would. The baby was created by Tim Webber and his team.
One visual model Cuarón had in mind for this violent, run-down vision of Britain’s future was Stanley Kubrick’s A Clockwork Orange (1971), but there are also points where he and cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki specifically use real-world imagery. He gave the art department images from “Sri Lanka, Iraq, Northern Ireland, Somalia, Chernobyl, the Balkans,” and he also pushed the largely English crew to “make it more Mexican.” That is, he wasn’t only relying on what people think a shabby futuristic England might look like, but using the film’s imagery to link a speculative near-future with the very real present.
A film’s story isn’t just told in what is shown on screen, but also in how it’s shown. That brings us to one of the most technically interesting aspects of Children of Men, which is its brilliant cinematography.
One thing worth mentioning is how much of the film uses natural lighting. Cuarón and Lubezki didn’t want the film to look stylized or futuristic; they wanted it to look like a documentary of the here and now. So Lubezki used as little artificial lighting as he could get away with, which meant altering some scenes from night to day to allow more light, or sometimes waiting for the fickle English weather to be more favorable. The film isn’t particularly dark or hard to see, because the lack of light is never used to obscure or muddle what’s on screen. It’s treated as part of the environment, so we see the characters as though they are moving through the world.
This is further emphasized by the film’s paucity of closeups. Most of it is filmed from something of a distance, with handheld cameras giving the sense of news or documentary footage. When there are closeups, it’s often because the characters are very close to each other, such as when five of them are jammed into that tiny Fiat.
And then there are those famously long shots, one of the things Children of Men is best known for.
A lot of people with a lot more patience than me have studied individual shot length in movies throughout history and around the world. There are some interesting broad trends: shots in the silent era were trending quite short (four to six seconds) before sound slowed things down, but in general shots have been getting faster and faster since then. The average length of shots depends very much on which countries you look at; Indian movies are infamously rapid-fire, some with shots every one to two seconds, adding up to thousands of shots. Action movies, no matter where they come from, also tend to have a very large number of very quick changes. We’ve watched some films from the other end of the spectrum; Stanley Kubrick loved to make movies with fewer long shots and it’s obvious in both A Clockwork Orange and 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968). But for the most part, especially in movies made more recently than the ’60s or ’70s, it’s pretty normal for a film to have 1000-2000 shots, with a common length of four to six seconds each.
Children of Men is 109 minutes long and contains just 460 shots. That gives the film an extremely long average shot length, especially for an action film that uses handheld cameras. It’s even more insane when you realize that the longest shots are among the most dynamic in the film, with the most action and violence.
Now, before anybody gets geared up to “well, actually” me, I will clarify that Children of Men has a number of extremely long apparent single shots that are made up of shorter—but still unusually long!—shots composited together using VFX. A relatively simple example of combining shots to create an apparent long shot is the coffee shop explosion at the very beginning of the film. The camera meets Theo as he enters the crowded coffee shop, then follows him out onto the street, then captures the explosion behind him. In reality, that shot was filmed on two separate days, with the explosion on the second day blowing up the same location on the same street, but now (obviously) empty.
That’s pretty straightforward compared to the wildly impressive scene later in which the characters are in a car that’s ambushed on a rural country road. It looks like a single shot. It really does. Go back and watch it. It looks like a single shot, even though we know it would be physically impossible to shoot that in a single take. It features five characters talking over each other in a small car interior, numerous attackers coming at the car from every direction, and camera motions that travel over and around and through the car. And it lasts for over six minutes. It was in fact filmed in six different chunks over the course of a week—including some parts where Cuarón, Lubezki, and a camera operator were actually strapped to a rig on top of the car. All of those pieces had to be matched, adjusted, and connected to achieve the seamless look that ends up on screen.
But the scene I find most incredible is the nine-minute shot near the end of the film, which starts when Theo and Kee are separated by the Fishers in the refugee camp, follows Theo through gunfire and explosions as he goes after Kee, through a crowded building until he finds her, then follows them again as he escorts her out of the building while both soldiers and refugees fall silent with awe at the sight of Kee’s newborn baby.
It’s an astonishing scene. Everything about it is breathtaking. The city is falling into chaos, gunfire and shouting and explosions fill the soundscape, the handheld camera first swings between characters like a witness trying to follow a conversation, then races and ducks and dodges along with Theo as he flinches, crawls, and stumbles his way through the warzone. Absolutely nothing about the scene is scripted or filmed to feel heroic. It’s desperate and terrifying, there are people injured and dying everywhere, and we can barely keep track of where we are. There’s no safety in moving from the open streets into the building, because the building is under attack and people are dying in the hallways. When Kee’s baby begins to cry, a stunned, breathless quiet spreads through the building and through the scene.
But the hushed awe doesn’t last. It’s broken by another explosion, and the fighting starts all over again.
It’s not clear from various sources exactly how much of that scene is a single continuous take, but Cuarón and Owen have both spoken about how it took weeks of preparation to get everything ready, and hours of setup for every time they wanted to record a take. If the camera operator tripped six minutes in, they would start over. The moment where blood splashes on the camera lens was unintentional; Cuarón said he tried to stop the take to start over, but because of the explosions nobody heard him and they kept recording. They left the blood on the lens for some of the final scene, but the take is not actually cut when the blood vanishes; they had a visual effects artist remove the droplets digitally for the second part of the scene.
Cuarón and Lubezki filmed as much of the movie in single takes as they could, and used digital effects to seamlessly combine what they could not, because the goal was never to show off their single-take virtuosity. The goal was something a lot more visceral.
Those long shots are the movie’s way of saying: Don’t look away. There’s so much pain and cruelty and suffering. Don’t look away. The world mourns the senseless death of a teenager while people die in the streets. Don’t look away. The rich surround themselves with treasures while there are people crammed into cages. Don’t look away. The violence might pause for a child but it certainly isn’t going to stop. The men with guns don’t care if you are a citizen with the right papers. This dystopia looks exactly like places you’ve seen on the news. These refugees look just like the ones your own governments treat so badly. Don’t look away.
I love this movie. It’s exquisitely crafted, and it provides a smart, incisive look at the world that manages to be contemporary and timeless, even twenty years later. I know I’m not the only one who feels this way; the movie received near-universal praise upon release and remains beloved. Children of Men is still one of the absolute best sci fi movies of the 21st century.
One particularly brilliant aspect I keep thinking about is how the movie ends. We don’t know what will become of Kee and her baby. We don’t know what will become of the world. We have absolutely no idea what, if anything, will change. Because the movie isn’t about that. Even though the film has the structure of an action film, with a recognizable male star at its center, it is not offering the comforting, simplistic fantasy that a white man’s heroic actions will immediately and noticeably save the world. We want to think Kee and her baby will change things, but we don’t know for sure because the future is—quite literally, in the final scene—shrouded in fog.
Children of Men is instead offering a more fragile, but ultimately more valuable, perspective: There is hope in trying to make the world better, even for one young woman and her child, even in the face of overwhelming obstacles, even if you won’t live to see the outcome.
So what do you think of Children of Men? Great movie, right? It’s such a great movie. Watching it again after some years was such a treat.
A Smorgasbord of Mindfuckery
For November and early December, we’ll be watching a handful of films that don’t fit together but also don’t quite fit anywhere else. What they have in common is that I’ve been shuffling them around my list for ages because I wasn’t sure when to watch them.
November 4 — Cube (1997), directed by Vincenzo Natali
This one was suggested way back when I first started this column and has been on the list ever since, but it turns out “Canadian horror movies about people trapped in giant homicidal mazes” is a rather limited niche.
November 11 — Brazil (1985), directed by Terry Gilliam
This could be a leftover from our October theme of movies about the near future, but it’s also very much its own thing that defies classification.
November 18 — Wax, or the Discovery of Television Among the Bees (1991), directed by David Blair
Another one that was suggested very early on. I can barely even figure out what it’s about from descriptions and articles, or even if it’s about anything at all. I’m happy to watch it anyway. It may or may not feature bees. Or television.
December 2 — Memories (1995), directed by Koji Morimoto, Katsuhiro Otomo, and Tensai Okamura
I don’t really know where to put an animated anthology collection of three short films, so we’ll just go ahead and watch it now.
December 9 — Donnie Darko (2001), directed by Richard Kelly
You know what they say: Nothing in life guaranteed except death and rabbits.

articles.title: A Bit about Email
articles.body:
A bit about email — First, some terminology; A typical email will past through many different components on the way to the recipient: 1. Sender's MUA [Via SMTP on port 465] 2. Sending MSA 3. Sending MTA[Via SMTP on port 25] 4. Receiving MTA 5. Receiving LDA and message store[Via IMAP] 7. Receiver's MUA (These aren't all necessarily different machines or even different programs, but it is helpful to name each step.) The mail user agent (MUA) runs on the user's computer and is what they use to send or read messages. Let's say they send something: that message will be uploaded to to the submission agent (MSA) which checks the user's password before handing off to the mail transfer agent (MTA). The transfer agent's job is to talk to other mail servers and get the message to the receiving side's MTA. Once received, it's given to the local delivery agent (LDA) to be stored until the recipient checks their email. The name "LDA" is non-standard, but I use it to avoid having four different abbreviations differing by a single letter. The reason for this structure is that when the system was being designed (around 1980), most organizations could only afford a single server. Maintenance was a full time job and updates often required multiple days of downtime. A well-connected computer might have dedicated single-digits megabit/second link that worked half the time. This forced the MTA and MUA distinction: if the recipient's server isn't up when the email is set, the sending MTA will save the message and re-attempt delivery later. This way, short outages don't cause bounced mail. Since the mail client is an interactive program the user runs, a separate message store is needed to keep the email until it can be read. Most MTAs are configured to continue retrying a message for five days, usually with exponential backoff: mine will wait 5 minutes after the first failure, and increase the interval to one hour in prolonged outages. The MSA and LDA have always existed in some capacity, but have gotten a lot more complicated when people started accessing email from their own computers instead or remotely logging onto a server. SMTP Most communication happens over the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, including MTA-MTA delivery. To narrow it down a bit, I'll pretend do be an MTA sending email to blog@maurycyz.com. The first step is to look up the receiving MTA for that domain: # dig MXmaurycyz.com [snip] maurycyz.com. 300 IN MX 1 smallcrow.com.[snip] #dig Asmallcrow.com [snip] smallcrow.com. 300 IN A 65.109.172.162[snip] Email is old enough to have it's own dedicated DNS record instead of using subdomain hacks or TXT abuse. The number is a priority (smaller is higher), which is used if multiple hosts are specified: a big email provider will have multiple servers to ensure timely delivery. SMTP is a relatively straightforward text based protocol. The one catch is that most mail servers will require a CRLF as a data terminator. This can often be sent with ctrl-m, but using a tool that automatically inserts cartridge-return bytes is easier: # telnet telnet> set crlf Will send carriage returns as telnet .telnet> open smallcrow.com 25Trying 65.109.172.162... Connected to smallcrow.com. Escape character is '^]'. 220 smallcrow.com ESMTP Postfix HELO nowhere 250 smallcrow.com MAIL FROM: 250 2.1.0 Ok RCPT TO: 250 2.1.5 Ok DATA 354 End data with . From: To: Hello, world.. 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as C870D7CD93 QUIT 221 2.0.0 Bye Each line sent is a command, to which the remote server responds with a three digit number followed by a human readable explaintaion. 200 responses mean it worked, 300 is "carry on...", 400 indicates temporary errors which tell the sender to try again later, 500 errors indicate that the email should be returned as un-deliverable. (If this seems similar to HTTP, that's no coincidence. A lot of the web, including its header syntax, was lifted from SMTP) The first command is always HELO (or EHLO), followed the sending MTA's hostname. This is usually not the same hostname that's in an email address, but many providers require it to match the sender's IP address. . The next two, MAIL FROM and RCPT TO specify the address to deliver to, and the address for any failure notifications. Bounce messages are usually generated one step up from where the error occurred: in most cases the receiving MTA has a problem and sends an error code to the sending MTA, but by that time MSA has already disconnect, forcing an emailed notification. Those notification themselves use an empty MAIL FROM to avoid infinite loops. Once the address has been specified and accepted, a DATA command is sent, followed by the actual message. This, at a minimum, contains the "From" and "To" headers along with some text. The message is terminated with a lone period to which the server replies to indicate that the message was sucessfuly handed off. Final hop MTAs should forward the email to the LDA before sending back a status code. This ensures that they never accept a message which they can't deliver, which would result in a error notification. This "backscatter" message interacts badly with spammers that forge MAIL FROM: it turns their obviously bogus message into one that is likely to be delivered and cause a nusance. There is no requirement for the addresses inside the email to match the ones in MAIL FROM and RCPT TO (also known as the envelope). The most common cause of this is a mail that has been forwarded. For example, a mailing list will set the envelope destination to match each member's email, but keep the original "From" and "To" headers intact so that replies work correctly. The envelope from will usually be changed to point to somewhere the list administrator will check for error notifications. Now, it's not that intermediate systems don't modify the headers: Most stages will add a "received" header to record where they got the message. While required for MTA to MTA communication, SMTP is used throughout the whole system. The mail client submits email using a different port, but over the same protocol. Communication between internal components (i.e. MTA to LDA) often uses the closely related Local Mail Transfer Protocol: the main difference is the assumption that the receiver doesn't have a message queue and will either deliver the mail immediately or return an error. Submission usually uses TLS to port 465, with the addition of a password (in base64): AUTH PLAIN 334 AGh1bnRlcgBodW50ZXIy 235 2.7.0 Authentication successful The one thing that's significantly different is the MUA's fetch, which operates on a "pull" basis. I won't go into the syntax here, but it's not terribly complicated. ... but if you actually try sending an email to, say, gmail, based on what I've written so far, it won't work. Some of that is due to them enforcing things like the Message-Id header: a unique identifier used to de-duplicate mail in cases where the receiving MTA accepts an email but the connection drops before the sender is informed about this. This causes the sender to try again later, which duplicating the message. However, a big part of it is... Authentication Base SMTP trusts that every sender is be well behaved: anyone can send email as anyone else. In fact, many hosts were configured to accept and relay mail from anyone as a conveyance for when someone's usual server was down. The original solution to bad behavior was to get the culprit kicked off the internet... but that fell apart quickly once the network grew and companies began getting involved: the first documented case of spam email was sent in 1978 and sold 13 million dollars in computers. While authentication doesn't prevent spam, it makes it possible to filter out unwanted senders. Verifying sender addresses is not possible using the MX record, since there is no guarantee the same host is used for receiving and sending mail. The simplest solution is to publish the sending address in a seperate DNS record: @ TXT v=spf1 ip4: 65.109.172.162 ip6: 2a01:4f9:c011:841a:b01d::1 -all; Roughly: ; allow from 65.109.172.162 ; allow from 2a01:4f9:c011:841a:b01d::1 ; deny otherwise However, that's not quite enough for the email empire. Big-tech also wants the email body to be signed with a cryptographic key published via a (DKIM) DNS record. This requires adding a step to sending mails, usually as a plugin for the MTA. While I rag on big-tech a lot, but this is actually a sensible policy: SPF can only verify the MAIL FROM, since forwarding the email will chance the source IP address. DKIM signatures are attached to the message and can be used to verify the original sender (the "From" address) of a message, which is what's actually shown to the user in most cases. However, both of these don't actually prevent spam, because spammers can just set up a few TXT records. Big-tech also requires the sender's HELO hostname to be consistent with their IP address, via both forward and reverse DNS. This helps prevent compromised devices from spewing out junk: a smart TV is unlikely to have a meaningful PTR record, and if it does, that hostname won't resolve back to it's address. ... unfortunately this policy also makes it impossible to directly send mail from most residential internet connections unless you own the address block. Of course, the solution is to pay a big-tech company money to relay your emails. If you don't like this, find a mail provider with more permissive rules: the only reason big-tech is able to keep their racket running that five or so companies control 99% of email. The message This is where SMTP stops being so simple. Let's look at the simplest possible email once it's been delivered: Return-Path : Delivered-To : bob@here Received : fromhere byhere with LMTP id bs05E10S7Go4VQMAHrglgg (envelope-from ) for ; Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:21:33 +0000DKIM-Filter : OpenDKIM Filter v2.11.0here B05E67CD18Received-SPF : None (mailfrom) identity=mailfrom; client-ip=313.33.33.337 ; helo=there ; envelope-from=alex@there ; receiver=here Received : fromthere (unknown [313.33.333.337 ]) byhere (Postfix) with SMTP id B05E67CD18 for ; Thu, 05 Nov 2026 05:20:42 +0000 (UTC)From : alex@there To : bob@here Hello, World! The format of the headers is superficially similar to HTTP headers, except that no line should exceed 78 bytes. (without the CRLF line terminator) Overlong headers are broken up and newly created lines are prefixed with whitespace to indicate that they are a continuation of the last header. Mail software generally preppends headers to the start of a message, so it's helpful to read them backwards. "From" and "to" are fairly self explanatory. Next, the "received" header contains a note from the receiving MTA: it includes the source's HELO name, IP address, RCPT TO and a timestamp. The MTA then performed SPF and DKIM checks, which came up empty: There's no signature and the MAIL FROM hostname is not publically resolvable. The LDA added another "received" header, although it's not very helpful. More importantly, it tacked on the "return-path" with the original MAIL FROM address and recorded the mailbox the message was delivered to. However, the body isn't always plain text. This is an email that includes formatting: [...] MIME-Version : 1.0Content-Type : multipart/alternative; boundary=----IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8XContent-Transfer-Encoding : 7bit------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X Content-Type : text/plain; charset=utf-8Content-Transfer-Encoding : quoted-printable Hello, World! I can do bold text!------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X Content-Type : text/html; charset=utf-8Content-Transfer-Encoding : quoted-printable
Hello, world! I can do bold<= /b> text
------IX71FHL6PHA0538LS1WKT2W9SF7S8X-- That's right, it's a web page! However, since not all email clients can understand HTML, the message also includes a plain text version. This is done using MIME's "multipart" encoding, in this case, multipart/alternative, which indicates all the versions are functionally equivalent. MIME's version number has been stuck at 1.0 since 1996. The delimiter is a randomly chosen string, which allows multiple multiparts to be nested inside without escaping. Each section of the message has it's own headers, in this case, indicating that it's sent in the quoted-printable encoding. This allows the email message to contain any bytes without exposing the MTA to scary things like non-seven-bit ASCII: remember, the SMTP is 45 years old. In quoted-printable, equal signs are used as the escape character: if followed by two hex digits, it decodes to that byte. If followed by a newline, both characters are removed. This is used to break long lines that could otherwise cause trouble. In this email, "=3D" becomes a literal equal sign and both lines are joined together. If you've ever seen an email with stray equals or missing one or two characters ~ every 80 bytes, broken quoted-printable decoding is usually the culprit. The second "content-transfer-encoding" is base64, which is used for binary files like attached images: MIME-Version : 1.0Content-Type : multipart/mixed; boundary="5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr"Content-Disposition : inline--5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr Content-Type : text/plain; charset=us-asciiContent-Disposition : inline Check out this file:--5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr Content-Type : application/octet-streamContent-Disposition : attachment; filename="file.bin"Content-Transfer-Encoding : base64 J7mtSdbQItOAi345nwaNkkTXrnDIRPA0DSwhbSAOwm2C/KoHjQIotY9lnJRMBRk9InQaHOxL bb7DGd9EN6uRpjvCbox9xblAh3CxH7sl+YAkYcKw1V100RpBwMhgaXfUJBB3oRkLffgRwEyK v9qFBLp9zZ+SiRJoRWbA4aZLexPhHZ35vFROVKYtiAeMlD1s15v3kPZvEADam0e45BoSaqmp 1S3z3b5wBIFHJUxQULD589MKaFx2Z2A+91pl/pbZWmZkzt55D/hZ05kjUUbXUnDnTYAQE2Gk WnN+SnrQvfEO+Tz7AdrbLD1q2DgwWW+k0cVJLKjdwRxesGhAkQCZfHVrno6R4iXjTbInIbQv hXzQiV840iUiUhk282WADd1ffJ0sot2Waf7XHLIE1lZVFQ3iGofYbw8pZlg3sb35AnIWPZKv fbC6Yh95RV23R4K2NHeBX1rpl4bSSiftnD2RbsBzv7cgw/6M/Lj3O40NFGAaUC+J7TpAaXdi tvlPsNQhMo8QRf/ub7WK42cPUlz1fKq1k1pzGN96YOsE5azMfF4vLANtbtbVmLIp2WmgBk0P 9IGMWy/xIAe0cOh+bqzru2+ojJGgx9uX4VSTP9BaTOwkVX5+rQfpp1qJodtHiO8sHw6Pg+Mg WcpqQPC7118ccuT44cVpIRkwOSoJzsW++WM=--5ZTNvId/H+rlk7Fr-- This is why size limits are often disappointing: the email will be 33% larger than the attached file. More efficient encodings (raw binary data) are supported by some MTAs, but may have to be converted to base64 somewhere down the path... which would break DKIM signing. Generally: - No encoding ("7-bit") can be used if the message has short lines and fits in low-bit ASCII. However, "7-bit" is mostly seen as a null encoding for already encoded multipart containers. - Quoted-printable if the message is mostly text, but has something that risks breaking ancient software. - Base64 for binary data. About TLS The SSL/TLS used by mail clients is effectively the same as for a browser: the mail provider must go to a certificate authority, prove their identity and get a certificate.. Algorithms and ciphers are disabled at the slightest hint they may be insecure. However, MTAs operates on "trusted" networks... although it's less that an attacker can't get access to internet traffic, but that if they could, it would be possible for them to pass an ACME challenge and take out a trusted certificate. As a result, the goal is mostly to protect against passive eavesdropping: most sysadmins don't bother dealing with a CA and use self-signed certificates. (it's not like CAs have a good track record: 4) Another weird thing about email is that MTAs don't use a separate TLS port. All connections on port 25 start as plaintext, then the sender issues a STARTTLS command and hands over the connection to a SSL/TLS library. It's somewhat janky, but it allows servers to attempt to use encryption and cleanly fall back if it's not supported. Such an approach isn't great for submissions, since a fall back would leak the password... and baddies on shared networks or nosy residential ISPs can strip out the STARTTLS command. For this case, it's best to default use the dedicated SSL submission port: 465. (This port actually has a bit of a history, with it being deprecated in favor of STARTTLS before being re-endorsed once we realized using optional SSL for passwords was a bad idea.) So what?? Unless you write email related software or run infrastructure, most of this information is profoundly useless. However, there are a few things you might want to remember. The underlying protocols allow five days for delivery, and it can sometimes take longer. Since users expect delivery in seconds and most emails are at least somewhat time sensitive, some MTAs are configured to send out delay notification if a message is taking a while. You may want to find out if yours does this before assuming the recipient is ignoring you. Emails are digital postcards. A message will be stored and forwarded by multiple systems in plaintext. Anyone on the network path may be able to read your email: SSL/TLS is not universally supported and can trivially be stripped out by active attackers. This is an inherent part of email: there's no way to tack-on strong encryption without breaking existing clients. If you need a guarantee of privacy, you must encrypt the message before sending, and the recipient must decrypt it themselves. Be careful with built-in tools like PGP: these generally make it way too easy to accidentally hit "reply-all" without encrypting, in addition to other flaws like exposing the subject line. PGP stuff Since publication, multiple people have written to me explaining how obfuscating the subject line (or warning if the user fills it out) is completly unreasonable to expect from a for a self-proclaimed privacy tool. At least in my eyes, "encrypted messaging" means encrypted, not 90% encrypted and 10% plaintext. The lack of deniablity and forward secrecy can be excused as limitiations of email's store-and-forward architecture... but default plaintext and making no attempt to encrypt certain the subject line or attachments is a recipe for disaster: at least with vanilla email, people know it is not encrypted. "Encrypted" email providers are largely snake oil. While the message store can encrypt messages and a custom MUA could decrypt them, the MTA must have access to plaintext. As a result, it provides minimal to no security against most attack vectors despite the "millitary grade encryption". The only way to fix email would be to get everyone to agree to switch to an end-to-end encrypted protocol... but the whole point of email is universal compatability: encrypted messaging can exist, but encrypted email is contradictory. The best hope is to find a mail provider that can be trusted not to snoop messages. That is to say, not an Advertising company (google) or one that's been pushing hard for LLMs (microsoft / apple): both of these businesses create strong incentives to read your messages. Although you'll still have to hope whoever you are communicating with isn't beign snooped on by their provider. Worse, DKIM signatures act as a lifelong proof that an email came from your provider's servers, even if a message is years old and has no clear chain of custody. This makes leaked, hacked, or snooped emails ideal extortion material: since the bad actor can trivially prove they haven't been fabricated. This property, called non-repudiation, is generally not desirable for private messaging systems. Avoiding signing not an option if you want to interoperate with big-tech, but it is possible to regularly rotate and publish private keys. Before they key is published, the signature can be trusted to verify it is legitimate. However, once the key has been published, the signature can been forged by anyone and is rendered retroactively untrustworthy. Since authentication is checked during delivery by the MTA and LDA, this doesn't affect how the email will be handled. However, it will cast doubt on the authenticity of leaked messages since the signature could have been forged with minimal effort. While key rotation is common practice, most mail providers don't publish their old private keys, so the signature is still trustworthy (modulo the service being hacked). I would advise against emailing something you wouldn't be comfortable reading out in public. Related: - https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc821/: Original SMTP - https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc2045/: MIME extended message format - https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7208/: SPF Authentication - https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6376/: DKIM signing

articles.title: Trump Backs Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Amid Chinese Spy Affair Investigation
articles.body:
Trump Backs Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Amid Chinese Spy Affair Investigation (apnews.com) 7
			
		 	
				President Donald Trump says the FBI is investigating Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman alleged by U.S. intelligence to have gathered information for Beijing. "I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump said at a White House briefing. The Associated Press reports:  Trump suggested the extraordinary step of directly involving himself in a counterintelligence investigation, a sign of his friendly relationship with Huang and the possible geopolitical stakes. "I did speak to him today just to see if he's feeling all right, how you're doing," Trump said. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."
Trump is slated to meet next week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, but he was noncommittal about bringing up the situation with Xi. "No, I don't think so," Trump said. "I mean, maybe. I'm sure President XI will ask me about it. I just know Jensen very well. I just think he's a very honorable man."
  Nvidia has launched its own independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Meanwhile, China has denied the allegations. "The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said during a regular news briefing Monday.
Further reading: Commerce Dept. Chip Inquiry Was Halted After Nvidia Intervention

articles.title: A short seller flagged Nvidia CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy six months before the scandal
articles.body:
Six months before the Nvidia spy scandal emerged, the New York-based short seller firm Culper Research had already raised questions about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unusually close relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that buys Nvidia chips. She is now suspected to be a Chinese spy.
The Nvidia CEO admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and the company has now opened a formal investigation into his relationship with Alice Huang (who shares his last name but is not related). U.S. intelligence officials believe she was recruited by the Chinese government to collect intelligence on Jensen Huang and influence his position regarding U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips.
Culper’s May 13 report is resurfacing because it picked up on the connection between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang while investigating Megaspeed’s ties to Nvidia.
In particular, the report called the relationship between the two executives “uncomfortably close,” noting that the Nvidia CEO was spotted partying and socializing with Alice Huang on multiple occasions. The report even claimed that some Nvidia employees wondered whether they had a “special relationship.”
Culper Research also theorized the China business that Nvidia lost to export controls had been rerouted through Southeast Asia, and that Megaspeed, a major chip buyer in the region, was secretly financed by Chinese tech giant Alibaba through shell companies. It pointed to financial records that showed Megaspeed’s total liabilities and equity had grown from $33 million at the end of 2023 to around $3 billion by the end of 2024, much of it in the form of refundable deposits from an unidentified source.
Financial Times reported Monday that documents show Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed through subsidiaries.
Culper is a short seller, so it stood to financially benefit from making these allegations, and those about possible illegal chip diversion have not been independently verified. Its report is available on the web and was posted to X back in May.

articles.title: Apple capped engineers at a $200 daily AI budget
articles.body:
Stork AI Daily/November 2026/Sunday, November 8, 2026
Apple capped engineers at a $200 daily AI budget.
By Wren Calloway·Reads 40 AI newsletters a day so you only read one.
TL;DR
- Apple has reportedly capped the daily AI spending budget for some of its engineers at $200.
- University of Michigan researchers found non-English prompts consume up to 179 times more energy.
- Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in talks to acquire AI security startup Clutch for $500 million.
- OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber to help approved security testers find vulnerabilities and build exploits.
- An obscure SSH edge case on Alpine Linux turned a standard account lock into a root-access trap.
- TokenEconomizer tracks coding-agent sessions to drastically cut wasted token spend on specific repos.
Apple has reportedly slashed the daily AI spending limit for some of its own engineers, dropping the cap from $300 down to $200. The internal reduction points to a stark reality that nobody in Cupertino wants to admit out loud: the company's AI expenditures are threatening to blow past their allocated budgets, and leadership is pulling the emergency brake.
When the world's most valuable tech giant starts treating compute like rationed office supplies, the rest of the industry needs to pay immediate attention. This is not about Apple lacking the liquid cash to fund its internal development. It is about the fundamental, inescapable economics of generative AI at enterprise scale. Uncapped access to advanced models creates an exponential cost curve that will ruin profit margins, even for a hardware empire that prints money.
For working builders, the takeaway is brutal but entirely necessary. The days of throwing unlimited tokens at a messy problem just to see what sticks are rapidly coming to an end. If your current product architecture relies on brute-force inference without strict, automated cost controls, you are not building a sustainable business—you are building a financial time bomb. The next massive competitive advantage in the AI space will not just be raw capability. It will be extreme efficiency. Startups that figure out how to cache intelligently, route to smaller models, and optimize their prompts will survive the coming squeeze. The ones who assume compute will just keep getting cheaper are going to run out of runway long before they run out of ideas. If Apple is sweating the daily API bill, you should be terrified of yours.
Today's Fight
Apple cuts engineer AI budgets to $200 a day.
By Wren Calloway·The Daily
The richest company on earth is rationing compute. If Apple is sweating the internal API bill, your startup's token bloat is a fatal disease.
Apple has reportedly slashed the daily AI spending limit for some of its own engineers, dropping the cap from $300 down to $200. The internal reduction points to a stark reality that nobody in Cupertino wants to admit out loud: the company's AI expenditures are threatening to blow past their allocated budgets, and leadership is pulling the emergency brake.
When the world's most valuable tech giant starts treating compute like rationed office supplies, the rest of the industry needs to pay immediate attention. This is not about Apple lacking the liquid cash to fund its internal development. It is about the fundamental, inescapable economics of generative AI at enterprise scale. Uncapped access to advanced models creates an exponential cost curve that will ruin profit margins, even for a hardware empire that prints money.
For working builders, the takeaway is brutal but entirely necessary. The days of throwing unlimited tokens at a messy problem just to see what sticks are rapidly coming to an end. If your current product architecture relies on brute-force inference without strict, automated cost controls, you are not building a sustainable business—you are building a financial time bomb. The next massive competitive advantage in the AI space will not just be raw capability. It will be extreme efficiency. Startups that figure out how to cache intelligently, route to smaller models, and optimize their prompts will survive the coming squeeze. The ones who assume compute will just keep getting cheaper are going to run out of runway long before they run out of ideas. If Apple is sweating the daily API bill, you should be terrified of yours.
Source: bloomberg.com
The Rest of the Field
Non-English prompts use up to 179 times more energy.
The globalization of AI comes with a massive environmental tax. Building for an international audience just became an infrastructure nightmare.
Researchers at the University of Michigan have uncovered a staggering disparity in AI resource consumption. According to their findings, processing AI prompts in non-English languages consumes up to 179 times more energy than running the exact same prompts in English. Worse, this massive spike in power draw often results in lower accuracy.
This completely shatters the illusion of effortless multilingual AI. If you are building a product intended for a global user base, your compute costs and latency just became wildly unpredictable based entirely on the user's native language. The tokenization systems underlying modern models are heavily optimized for English, punishing everyone else with bloated token counts and agonizingly slow inference.
This is a disaster for localized SaaS. If a French or Japanese user costs you exponentially more to serve while receiving a worse product, the unit economics of global expansion are broken. Until the foundational models overhaul their multilingual tokenization, builders will have to heavily restrict non-English features or eat the massive efficiency loss.
Palo Alto Networks in talks to buy Clutch for $500M.
Agentic AI is a security nightmare waiting to happen, and enterprise defense giants are writing massive checks to plug the holes.
Palo Alto Networks is reportedly in discussions to acquire the cybersecurity startup Clutch for approximately $500 million. The specific goal of this massive proposed buyout is to enhance control over AI agents and strictly manage their access to internal company systems.
We are finally seeing the enterprise reaction to autonomous agents. Everyone wants AI that can take actions on their behalf, but nobody wants a rogue script hallucinating its way into the payroll database. Clutch built the exact guardrails that massive corporations need before they let agentic workflows touch their proprietary data, and Palo Alto is paying a premium to own that chokepoint.
If you are building autonomous tools for B2B clients, access control is no longer a feature—it is the entire product. The enterprise market is terrified of agentic sprawl. The startups that win will be the ones that can show their AI won't accidentally delete the production database when given a vague prompt.
Source: techcrunch.com
OpenAI releases GPT-6 Cyber to approved security testers.
The offensive AI arms race is officially productized. Handing automated exploit generation to testers is a massive escalation in the security wars.
OpenAI has officially launched GPT-6 Cyber, a restricted AI model specifically designed to identify software vulnerabilities and construct functional exploits. Access is currently strictly limited to approved security testers, keeping the offensive capabilities out of the public API for now.
This is a massive shift in how we approach software defense. We have moved from AI that suggests better code to AI that actively hunts for zero-days and writes the payload to break them. By productizing exploit generation, OpenAI is acknowledging that the only way to secure the next generation of software is to attack it with the same automated ferocity that malicious actors are already developing.
For working developers, the margin for error just vanished. If a commercially available model can automatically find and exploit vulnerabilities in your codebase, security through obscurity is dead. You now have to assume that every endpoint you expose will be instantly probed by an agent smarter than the engineer who wrote it.
Source: openai.com
Proton cancels staff AI re-interviews after employee revolt.
Interrogating your entire workforce about their prompt history is a fast track to losing your best talent.
Proton has abruptly canceled its planned AI-use re-interviews following significant internal pushback. The privacy-focused company had intended to question nearly all of its staff regarding how they use AI in their daily workflows, but widespread employee resistance forced leadership to scrap the initiative entirely.
This is a spectacular misread of company culture. Trying to audit the daily AI habits of your entire engineering and product org feels less like policy enforcement and more like a witch hunt. Developers are already using AI to write code, draft emails, and debug systems; threatening them with re-interviews only guarantees they will start hiding their usage instead of optimizing it.
The lesson here is simple: you cannot mandate transparency through intimidation. If you want to know how your team is utilizing new models, give them enterprise accounts and track the telemetry. Treating AI adoption as a suspicious activity to be interrogated is a guaranteed way to drive your top performers to a competitor who actually trusts them.
Source: 404media.co
Google introduces new school AI controls.
Google is forcing schools to choose between modern search and keeping AI out of the classroom, and the bundle is breaking.
Google has rolled out new AI controls specifically tailored for educational institutions. However, the update has sparked immediate debate over whether schools can actually retain access to traditional Google Search while selectively opting out of its deeply integrated AI functionalities.
The tech giant is running into the hard limits of forced adoption. By baking generative summaries directly into the core search experience, Google has created a nightmare for school administrators who want to prevent automated plagiarism without blocking the internet's primary research tool. The friction here shows that treating AI as an un-toggleable default doesn't work in highly regulated environments.
For builders, this is a masterclass in the dangers of feature coupling. If your core product is indispensable but your new AI features are controversial, tying them together doesn't force adoption—it forces churn. Users need the ability to downgrade to the deterministic version of your software, or they will simply find a provider who lets them turn the magic off.
The NFL partners with Carnegie Mellon for AI football analysis.
Sports analytics just moved from spreadsheets to computer vision. The team that trains the best model will own the draft.
The NFL has formed a direct partnership with researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, handing over extensive game film and proprietary player-tracking data. The collaboration is aimed at advancing AI development to fully automate the analysis of football strategy and player performance.
This is what happens when massive proprietary datasets meet specialized models. The NFL is sitting on decades of high-framerate, multi-angle telemetry that no one else has access to. By opening that vault to CMU, they are building the foundation for AI that can read defensive coverages and predict route running faster than any human scout.
The moat here isn't the algorithm; it's the data. If you want to build a truly defensible AI product, you need to find an industry that has been hoarding unstructured data for years and figure out how to parse it. The organizations that own the raw footage will dictate the future of automated analysis.
Source: instagram.com
Today's Highlights
research
Your iPhone Is Quietly Blocking These Phrases
Your iPhone is silently rewriting contradictory phrases without telling you why, exposing the keyboard as a black box.
Read more →
Automated testing accelerated the exploitation of a tiny edge case that turned Alpine Linux account locks into root access.
A brute-force experiment uses Claude to figure out what the original artist typed for a 32-pixel texture.
Sanskar Tiwari’s six-year micro-SaaS journey shows that launching multiple small bets is safer than risking everything on one idea.
Earning attention before launch and optimizing the paywall afterward is the real secret behind this subscription app's massive success.
A first-time hardware build exposes how quickly small physical details completely derail an AI's perfect theoretical code.
Tool of the Day
TokenEconomizer
If you are bleeding API credits every time your agent reads the same boilerplate, you need this installed yesterday. It solves the exact problem of context-window bloat by remembering what your agent actually needs to see. I would only skip this if your employer is still blindly paying your OpenAI bill.
TokenEconomizer learns from your coding-agent sessions to eliminate wasted token usage on repository-specific tasks.
More Worth a Look
- Compliance Papermark — Papermark secures data rooms for high-stakes deals with page-level analytics and granular, audit-friendly permissions.
- Marketing Superscale — Superscale generates video ads, copy, and creative assets to launch and iterate performance campaigns in minutes.
- Learning AskVideo — AskVideo transforms YouTube videos into interactive knowledge bases that provide timestamped answers to your questions.
- Design MagicSlides — MagicSlides generates structured presentations and slide content directly from text prompts and various document inputs.
- Media Movavi Video Editor — Movavi Video Editor offers fast, easy-to-use software for editing photos and videos safely across platforms.
The Bottom Line
By the end of Q1, at least two major cloud providers will introduce strict, hard-capped token budgeting tools natively as enterprise AI bills trigger a wave of CFO panic.
Keep your context windows tight and your API keys hidden.
— Wren Calloway · Stork AI Daily

By baking generative summaries directly into the core search experience, Google has created a nightmare for school administrators who want to prevent automated plagiarism without blocking the internet's primary research tool. The friction here shows that treating AI as an un-toggleable default doesn't work in highly regulated environments.
For builders, this is a masterclass in the dangers of feature coupling. If your core product is indispensable but your new AI features are controversial, tying them together doesn't force adoption—it forces churn. Users need the ability to downgrade to the deterministic version of your software, or they will simply find a provider who lets them turn the magic off.
The NFL partners with Carnegie Mellon for AI football analysis.
Sports analytics just moved from spreadsheets to computer vision. The team that trains the best model will own the draft.
The NFL has formed a direct partnership with researchers at Carnegie Mellon University, handing over extensive game film and proprietary player-tracking data. The collaboration is aimed at advancing AI development to fully automate the analysis of football strategy and player performance.
This is what happens when massive proprietary datasets meet specialized models. The NFL is sitting on decades of high-framerate, multi-angle telemetry that no one else has access to. By opening that vault to CMU, they are building the foundation for AI that can read defensive coverages and predict route running faster than any human scout.
The moat here isn't the algorithm; it's the data. If you want to build a truly defensible AI product, you need to find an industry that has been hoarding unstructured data for years and figure out how to parse it. The organizations that own the raw footage will dictate the future of automated analysis.
