articles.title: Borrowing a Microsoft-signed shim to abuse Secure Boot on corporate hardware
articles.body:
Created on Sun. 08 Nov 2026
Halli hallo everyone, this blog post is a continuation of the p3ng0s series that has been going on on this blog for a few years. This is my latest research on how secure boot works that I did back in April of this year and this blog post is a tease for p3ng0s V2 release that will happen probably in 1 Year from now.
Before I start on this post I want to explain something really quick I will focus the rest of this year and early next year on finishing maldev academy writing a small research paper on PIC malware and doing CRTO 1 + 2. I really want to add a bunch of stuff to p3ng0s but first I need to finish the stuff I just mentioned so that I am not mentally distracted when doing p3ng0s V2. I really wan't to push the physical security side of the OS and I have a bunch of great ideas. This secure boot work that I'm gonna explain here is a direct parallel to this work. It was an idea I had in the middle of developing V1 but I pushed it back too V2 to avoid scope creep and then ended up implementing it anyway on a V2 branch. So if you like this post you can use this technique right now, a mini tutorial is mentioned at the end of the post here.
Before going to much into the weeds of secure boot let me just put this out here. Before doing this research I personally knew nothing exactly about secure boot. To me it actually just was this annoying BIOS option that blocked me from booting into linux when I bought a new laptop, I knew it was a Microsoft pushed thing and because of that I was never very happy of buying hardware and having to disable this feature to then use the computer how I wanted. You reading this post I would like you to take a minute to think about the following questions, obviously this works best if like me your knowledge of secure boot was limited: what you think secure boot actually is? What do you think this feature is actually for? Why does it exist?
Great so after some thinking my conclusion before reading up about secure boot in detail was to lock down what operating system is running on the machine. I thought well there's these keys that say okay this OS can boot this OS cannot more or less. And that you needed specific keys to boot and those where microsoft controlled. This answer is close but not exactly right. The actual reason secure boot exists is for the following: Ensuring the integrity of the booting OS. Now the wording here is very important isn't ensuring integrity the same as locking to one booting OS? (at least that is how I would interpret that statement back then). Well turn's out not at all ensuring integrity means: Yes yes the signature of this OS is in the database of accepted OS and that is it.
Now some companies do allow employees to run linux right? Does that mean the CISO of those is just nuts and disables secure boot on his fleet? Turn's out that is a flat NO. There is this thing called Microsoft Corporation UEFI CA 2011 and is used to sign 3rd party operating systems that can work with Microsoft keys that are installed on 99% of BIOSes out there. Okay so turns out secure boot can just work with ANY keys you can just make your own enroll them in your BIOS and sign your linux build with them and that's it it will just work.
Here is a screenshot of the bazzite OS tutorial on enrolling their keys inside of your BIOS. Okay so now we understand 2 things: 1. Microsoft has 3rd party keys for some linux distributions, 2. If you can mess around in the BIOS you can just enroll your own keys. Now let's just sit with this and think what is secure about this? Like if I can just enroll my own keys how is this secure? Well turn's out secure boot was not to target consumers nor physical access to a machine, secure boot was only to stop one specific attack: EFI malware. Like if a malware is sitting on the EFI level and windows does not wipe EFI partitions on computer reset you have a "Immortal" malware excluding the fact that if you just wipe every partition this problem goes away but yeah that is besides the point.
Now so we know that Microsoft signs 3rd party OS for secure boot access but these OS are always changing and those keys don't change that often but the grub version the OS those things keep on moving so how come 1 key that never really changes unless expires changes but the software underneath changes all the time does that not break integrity of the boot chain? Well yes it does this is where something called a shim and MOK enrollement comes into play!
Okay here is a provided diagram of how MOK enrollment looks like. Do you see the issue that I have with this? To me it seems a bit trivial well if I can pick the keys during mok enrollment why not just pick my own keys? From there it's jackpot I booted my OS on hardware that has secure boot enabled! Okay so in the previous chain let me explain something clearly the BIOS has microsoft 3rd party keys installed, the shim is 3rd party microsoft signed if the grub image is signed with a unrecognized key the shim fails and boot's into this MOK software where you can PICK the key that matches the GRUB and linux signature.
Okay so like I mentioned a few times now this 3rd party program from Microsoft for those magic keys, who is in them? Turns out a few OS: ubuntu, debian, fedora and some others. These open source OS are well open source can't I find the shim and make my OS just stand as ubuntu? Like opsec wise this would be gold I make my "hacking" OS look like ubuntu on the secure boot chain and if the computer itself has those 3rd party certificates installed I win and can boot into a dropbox or whatever on the hardware of the place I am targeting.
Let me introduce you to my new favourite website pkgs.org a website where you can search for packages across multiple linux distributions! And when we search for a package named shim we can find something that I find hilarious! A package named shim-signed. Well well well what do you guys think I am going to do with those? Exactly we will borrow them ;)
          So what we need is the MOK software for enrolling our crap and we need well the actual
          shim signed by Microsoft. Really quick in this example I did skip something: how I know
          it's actually Microsoft signed here is the command to check: sbverify --list you_shim_file.efi
          and the output should have something similar:
        
Okay so since this is all BOOT adjacent things we need to actually mess around with EFI partitions and how things are actually booting. Quick note if you fuck up here well your drive / USB won't boot, hehehe happened to me a few times call it a right of passage! Right so to get the SHIM installed you will need to take your EFI partition and mount it! From there you should see the following files:
Start with generating your keys with the following command:
openssl req -newkey rsa:4096 -nodes -keyout "./MOK.key" -new -x509 -sha256 -days 3650 -subj "/CN=some name/" -out "./MOK.crt"
Once you have your keys make sure you sign your kernel with the keys
sbsign --key "./MOK.key" --cert "./MOK.crt" --output /boot/vmlinuz-linux /boot/vmlinuz-linux
          Side note to sign the kernel you cannot do that on a live USB unless you build it yourself.
          In the case of p3ng0s I specifically added a hook that does this during build time your can
          see it under the file airootfs/etc/pacman.d/hooks/zzzz98-mok-signing.hook of the V2 branch.
          But technically you can install for example kali linux directly to a USB drive: boot that drive and then sign that kernel
          then unboot the drive and do the EFI steps on that usb drive and you would have the same tech working on kali linux.
          Honestly to do this I recommend copy pasting this entire blog post into claude and asking him
          to generate you a tutorial and walk through that with him!
        
Okay next you need to rename the EFI file we found before to "grubx64.efi" and sign it:
mv ./BOOTx64.EFI ./grubx64.efi # rename
sbsign --key "/where_you_put_your_shim/MOK.key" --cert "/where_you_put_your_shim/MOK.crt" ./grubx64.efi --output ./grubx64.efi # sign grub
Okay after that you take your actual shim and name it "BOOTx64.EFI" and place the MOK software next to it:
cp -r "/path_to_your_shim/shimx64.efi" ./BOOTx64.EFI
cp -r "/path_to_your_shim/mmx64.efi" ./mmx64.efi
After that make sure you convert your certificates to a format secure boot will accept like so, and place the key inside of the EFI partition for quick access later:
openssl x509 -in "./MOK.crt" -outform DER -out ./borrowed-mok.der
This is what the EFI partition should finally look like inside of it's BOOT folder:
Okay now we have the drive primed and ready with our newly acquired Microsoft signed shim! The way this works is simple you have a laptop with well secure boot active and the Microsoft 3rd party certificates pre-installed (They are most of the time btw especially on corporate machines since well some software actually needs them on on windows. But also some don't have it installed HP wolf security for example was hit and miss some did some didn't, cutaway was maybe last year or 2 years where they stopped enabling it :P)
So in our case let's make it realistic we just plug in the drive and go inside of the BOOT from other device option usually F7 but it changes on some models of computers (NOTE: you don't need BIOS passwords for this option LOL). From here we select our newly created drive and we will boot the sim and fail the grub signing section and be present with the MOK enrollment software like so:
Here we select Enroll Key from disk and navigate to the BOOT/ folder where our key was put in the previous steps!
How we just say yes we want to enroll that key
Great and here we can just continue to boot and grub will just appear! Yeah so not so secure boot after all....
          Okay so if you want to use this on p3ng0s when you clone archlive make sure
          you do a git checkout on the V2 branch and before running
          the build command you need to place the shim and mok manager inside of the
          overlay/airootfs/etc/p3ng0s/shim folder!
          I did update the Live ISO.pdf file for p3ng0s that has the instructions
          on how to build the OS with the steps for secure boot it can be found
          here
          before I make V2 fully public and update the official documentation.
        
Well I hope you liked this little blog post on something I found kinda fun to poke at! I am thinking of expanding this blog to also feature some lockpicking in a bit once I get properly onto green belt for that. You can support the blog by getting my amazing merch on red bubble via the link on the side / bellow. Everything here is self made so please share around I obviously don't have a PR team. Any follow on github / linked-in twitter is welcome or you can just use the RSS feed directly from the home page of this blog there is a little button. Check out the other p3ng0s posts as well they are quite good. Or you can read-up on NTDLL-Reconstruction an EDR bypass technique I made after being inspired by Hell's Gate. Also if you have feedback message me directly on linked-in I answer questions since my blog is not famous I do answer.
If you like the content of my website you can get the amazing stickers from this websize. You can also support me through my github sponsors page.

articles.title: The race is on to sue Nvidia
articles.body:
Nvidia’s stock slid more than 4% on Monday, the first trading day after its board said it would investigate CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with Alice Huang, an executive U.S. intelligence believes was spying for China.
Securities lawyers were already moving. Schall, Brown & Schwartz, a Los Angeles shareholder-rights firm, was among the first to plant a flag, announcing Monday morning that it’s investigating whether Nvidia made false or misleading statements, or failed to disclose information pertinent to investors. Robert Bartlett, a Stanford Law professor and securities law expert, expects it to have plenty of company.
“I would definitely wager that there’ll be a filing,” Bartlett said in an interview, adding that he wouldn’t be surprised if a case had been filed by the end of day Monday. Plaintiffs’ lawyers have good reasons to be first in line; under federal securities law, the first complaint triggers a public notice, and investors then have 60 days to ask the court to be named lead plaintiff. A firm that files early gets a head start on signing up investors with large losses, as well as on shaping the story of the case. Nvidia is headquartered in Santa Clara, so it’s likely we’ll see this in the Northern District of California. (It’s very possible a case has already been filed; newly filed cases can take up to 24 hours to be discoverable online.)
While much remains unknown, the legal theory here doesn’t depend on anything the board’s investigation turns up about Huang’s private life. When The New York Times first reported on Huang’s ties to Alice Huang last month, the executive at the Singapore data center company Megaspeed, an Nvidia spokesperson described the relationship to another outlet, The Hill, as “not unusual or unexpected.” The company representative added, “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”
Since then, Huang has acknowledged to the board that the relationship was intimate. Meanwhile, The Times reports that U.S. intelligence had been monitoring Alice Huang for more than a year.
From a securities perspective, Bartlett said, the company’s earlier statement was “clearly a misleading statement.” And because Huang is CEO, Bartlett said, “his knowledge gets imputed to the company.” In other words, Nvidia is treated as having known what its chief executive knew.
Bartlett says the likely vehicle is a “classic fraud on the market” claim, in which investors argue they paid prices that reflected false or incomplete public information, and lost money when the truth emerged. Monday’s drop gives them a lot to work with. Damages in such cases are tied to the stock’s decline, and Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world, so you can imagine a settlement could prove exceedingly expensive.
The usual path is that the case is litigated for a long time and then settles, Bartlett notes. That means a large payment from the company and its directors-and-officers insurers, but typically no personal consequences for the CEO or the board. It is also a civil matter, so Huang isn’t facing prison over it. The irony, as Bartlett noted, is that the suit is brought in the name of Nvidia’s shareholders, and shareholders ultimately pay for the settlement, directly or through insurance premiums.
Bartlett sorted Nvidia’s wider exposure into buckets. The first is the securities fraud claim, which is the clearest immediate problem for the company and potentially for Huang. The second is governance: what the board knew and when. It’s possible directors were kept in the dark, but the board also has oversight duties, and once the Times began reporting on the Megaspeed connection, the company should have had reporting lines to bring a critical risk like this to directors. If it didn’t, or if directors didn’t act, board-level liability is possible.
A third category, one that would change everything, would arise only if the board’s investigation finds Huang knew about the intelligence connection. That would be “a whole other ball game,” as Bartlett said. (The board said in a statement to the public Sunday that it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.)
There’s also the question of government action. The SEC can seek an officer-and-director bar for intentional securities-fraud violations, which Bartlett said is technically on the table. But he doubted the current SEC under Chairman Paul Atkins would have the appetite, given President Trump’s support for Huang. A roughly two-year clock after discovery of the facts would leave room for a future administration to act, though the window would be tight, and Bartlett posited that’s pretty unlikely when asked about it.
It’s worth underscoring that an announcement like Schall, Brown & Schwartz’s is not on its own a sign of a strong case. SBS files a lot of “investigation” notices. A notice shows a plaintiff’s firm sees an opportunity. Which firm winds up leading the case is decided later by the court, and that decision usually depends on which investor has the largest loss.
Other firms that are lining up against Nvidia include Rosen Law Firm, Levi & Korsinsky, Bronstein, Gewirtz & Grossman, and The Law Offices of Frank R. Cruz. Each announced their own investigations Monday, and Rosen said it is preparing a class action lawsuit.

articles.title: The New Our Place Wonder Oven I Used Every Day for a Year Is on Early Sale for Black Friday
articles.body:
The New Our Place Wonder Oven I Used Every Day for a Year Is on Early Sale for Black Friday
I love a good kitchen countertop appliance. But I don’t have a ton of counter space for them all, so I have to be judicious about which ones get a permanent spot in my home. And one that will always have a special place in my kitchen is Our Place’s Wonder Oven Pro.
I’ve tried all three of Our Place’s Wonder Oven models, and this is far and away my favorite. Not only does it have a sleek touchscreen, but it also offers more functionality than the other two. And while it is a little pricey, it’s currently discounted for Our Place’s November sale that runs now through Monday, November 30. Don’t wait to take advantage of this great buy.
Our Place’s Wonder Oven Pro Is on Sale Ahead of Black Friday
You might already know Our Place as the kitchen brand behind the viral Always Pan. Our Place also offers bakeware, titanium pans (which I love), tableware, kitchen tools and accessories (like one of my favorite dish towels), and small appliances, like a blender, multicooker, and rice cooker (which I also love; can you tell I’m a fan?).
Of course, Our Place also has three different Wonder Ovens, which are air fryer toaster ovens. The smallest (and OG) Wonder Oven is a 6-in-1 appliance with a retro design down to the knob dials. The Large Wonder Oven came next, and it also has a 6-in-1 functionality, but it’s more spacious on the inside, so you could make a whole frozen pizza without having to turn to your oven.
Then, last fall, Our Place dropped it’s most souped-up model yet: the Wonder Oven Pro. Unlike older versions, it features a sleek touchscreen display and adds dehydrate and proof modes — making it an 8-in-1 device. You can also bake, roast, air fry, toast, broil, and reheat. Plus, a convenient cap on the top left allows you to add water, infusing steam into your food while it cooks (like toast, so it comes out crispy and fluffy).
The Wonder Oven Pro usually goes for $325, and while I think it’s absolutely worth the money, you can snag it for $275 right now during the brand’s November sale.
My Honest Review of Our Place’s Wonder Oven Pro After 1 Year
The Wonder Oven Pro was launched last September, and I got mine right around that time. So I’ve now had it for just over a year, and I can honestly say that I’m more in love with it than ever.
I was a fan when I first got it, but now it has become a staple in my kitchen. When I have to test other air fryers and air fryer toaster ovens as part of my job as a shopping writer, I daydream about when I can go back to using my Wonder Oven Pro. It’s truly beat out every other model I’ve tried.
It’s more versatile than other air fryer toaster ovens.
Part of the reason for this is how versatile this model is. I love all the functionality it offers, even if I do mainly use two or three functions. I use the toast preset every day for breakfast, and its default is set to 400°F for four minutes, which turns my bread and English muffins a perfect golden-brown.
The touchscreen is ultra-precise.
Beyond that, I also love how sleek and stylish this machine is. The touchscreen is so nice and allows me to be more precise than I could be with the dials that the other models have. Plus, this is the only model that comes in Pistachio, which looks cute on my counter.
It’s silent.
Oh, and one other very important feature for me? It’s not obnoxiously loud. I had a prior air fryer toaster oven that played a chime so weirdly long and loud, I always worried it would wake my family up (like I said, I primarily use it in the morning). But this one plays a short and not terribly loud jingle that gets my attention, but doesn’t bother the entire house.
So, if you’ve been thinking about upgrading to an air fryer toaster oven, there is only one that I’ve found that is truly worth the money and counter space: the Wonder Oven Pro. Do yourself a favor and snag it while you can save a little coin!
Buy: Our Place Wonder Oven Pro, $275 (on sale!) at Our Place
What’s your favorite air fryer toaster oven? Tell us about it in the comments below.

articles.title: Supply chain attack on Qubole customers
articles.body:
One Stolen Vendor Key, Every Customer’s Data Exposed: Inside the Qubole Supply Chain Attack
How a third-party compromise created a path into multiple organizations, and how Sentra uncovered it in less than 24 hours.
Co-authored with Sagy Drucker, Asaf Rozali and Riva Kranz
Sentra recently uncovered a very wide supply chain attack that moved through organization after organization. Dozens of Qubole customers were impacted. An attacker got hold of credentials belonging to Qubole, a big-data platform, and used the access that company after company had once granted Qubole to quietly pull their data. Nobody broke into these companies directly. The attacker came in through a vendor they all trusted.
This kind of risk is easy to miss. Your cloud is full of identities that aren't people: vendor integrations, automation and AI agents, each holding standing access to your data. Most days they do the same thing, from the same place, on the same schedule. The danger is the day one of them starts doing something else, and very few teams are watching for it.
The riskiest of these are the ones you forgot. Every vendor you have ever connected to your cloud left a door behind. Most of those doors are still there, trusted, rarely watched, and often able to reach your most sensitive data.
Sentra spotted the campaign and reported it to Wiz, which investigated it together with Sentra and Mandiant. Wiz has published the full research: Trusted by Default: Qubole Cross-Account Access Abused in the Wild.
This post isn't the story of one company. It's what we saw across the attacks: how the attacker got in, how they moved, what they went after, and what finally gave them away.
The attack at a glance
- More than a dozen organizations hacked in a single attack, all through access they had once granted Qubole.
- About a second to assume each Qubole-trusted role, so the attacker could move from one company to the next almost instantly.
- About 100 passwords and keys read in 7 minutes, from three different places they were stored, plus thousands of credential records inside the files the attacker downloaded.
- 0 write actions. Nothing was changed or deleted, only stolen, which made it harder to notice.
Forgotten vendor trust
The doors the attacker used were old ones. Qubole roles were still in place long after companies had stopped using Qubole, and those roles could read nearly all of the data the attacker went after.
Qubole's roles had been dormant since the spring. Then they came back to life. Sentra had seen this risk coming. Before the attack, it had already flagged one of Qubole's roles as unused for months yet still able to reach sensitive data.
Valid credentials, wrong network
The organizations hit by this attack weren't careless. They set up their Qubole integrations the way AWS recommends, including an additional check called an ExternalId, a code the vendor must present before it can get in. Every Qubole role had it, and the attacker presented the right code every time. As far as AWS could tell, the attacker was Qubole.
None of the activity came from Qubole's own network. It all came from a rented OVH server and the Mullvad VPN, and there was no normal Qubole activity at all in that window. Every session was the attacker.
That's what makes supply chain attacks so dangerous. When a trusted vendor is compromised, following best practice isn't enough, because the attacker's access is real and looks legitimate in every log. Only two things stop it. Zero trust limits each vendor to the data it truly needs, so a stolen key opens as little as possible. And data detection and response (DDR) watches how every identity actually uses data, flagging the moment a trusted one starts behaving like an attacker. In this attack, the access looked valid. The behavior didn't.
Test quietly, then sweep
The attacker started slowly. They tested the stolen credentials on one low-value Qubole role, took a quiet look around, and made a first theft of thousands of customer-profile files. Then they moved fast. Within minutes they entered every Qubole-trusted role and started bulk downloads that ran in the background over the following days. A final pass, from a different VPN address, pulled production database backups.
Then the activity stopped. The trusts were still in place, so the attacker went quiet without ever losing access.
How the attacker stole credentials
Stealing data wasn’t enough. We saw the attacker use several different techniques to steal credentials that could open even more doors:
- Pulling secrets in bulk from Secrets Manager: source-control, identity-provider, CI and database credentials, and even the vendor’s own tokens and ExternalIds.
- Reading decrypted parameters from SSM Parameter Store, including monitoring and scanner agent keys.
- Harvesting Lambda environment variables, switching to a second route when the first one was blocked.
- Scraping EC2 user data, the startup scripts where tokens and passwords often hide.
How we traced it
The first job was matching the leaked samples to data Sentra had already scanned. We compared what was inside the files, not just their names, because names are easy to change and content isn't.
Within a few hours we had it down to a handful of S3 buckets. Those were the sources, and the question became much narrower: who could read them?
Each source bucket could be reached by hundreds of identities: service roles, admins, single sign-on users and automation. Chasing every one of them in a day wasn't realistic. So we narrowed to external identities, the accounts outside a company's environment that are still trusted to get in, such as vendors, tools and partners. Then we checked which of them could read most of the source buckets. One stood out: Qubole.
Being able to reach data doesn't mean someone did. So for every external identity, we compared its activity to its own history: when it was used, how often, from which IP addresses, and what it did. Every vendor looked normal except one.
A small team split the work, each using AI to move faster, and we held every finding to one rule: it was either proven or assumed. That rule saved us more than once. One early lead looked strong on paper, but the activity logs showed the identity had never been used, so we dropped it.
Proving what was taken
Knowing the attacker could reach the data wasn't enough. Each affected company needed to know what was actually taken, and that's harder to prove than it sounds, because most cloud storage doesn't record every file read by default. So we pieced the picture together from three places.
The first was encryption. Every time an encrypted file is downloaded, the cloud has to unlock it, and each unlock is logged with the file's name. By matching those records to the attacker's sessions, we could see which files left. Files that only use default encryption leave no such trail, so the real number is likely higher.
The second was the secrets themselves. Every password and key the attacker read left its own record, which gave an exact list of what to change.
The third was file access logs. Where they were turned on, they recorded every file the attacker downloaded, with the IP and session. Across one company's accounts that came to millions of files, and on encrypted buckets the logs matched the encryption records exactly.
This is where having an agentic Data Security Platform makes the difference. Sentra continuously discovers and classifies sensitive data across cloud, SaaS, data warehouses, on-premises environments and AI systems. It also maps every employee, service account and AI agent to the data each one can reach. After a breach, the clock is running: breach notification deadlines can be as short as 72 hours, and every hour spent working out what was taken is an hour that can't be spent containing it. Logs can show which files were touched, but not what was inside them. Because Sentra had already discovered and classified our customers' data, we knew which locations held personal, financial and credential data before the investigation even began. That turned "what did we lose?" from a question that can take weeks into one we answered the same day.
Five actions, same day
By the end of the day, we could give each affected customer five clear actions, each backed by evidence:
- Remove Qubole from every role that trusts it.
- Rotate every secret that was read. We shared each secret's name and where to find it in their logs, without ever seeing the values themselves.
- Block the attacker's IP addresses.
- Preserve the logs before they expire.
- Let Qubole know.
One vendor, many targets
What we saw wasn't unique to one company. The attacker held Qubole's credentials, and those credentials opened a door at every organization that still trusted Qubole. This was a broad campaign that moved through company after company, impacting dozens of Qubole customers.
Because Sentra can see which organizations trust the same vendor, we checked every Sentra customer with a Qubole connection within about an hour. The same activity showed up across customer environments, a long-unused Qubole role suddenly waking up in the same window, and we warned each affected customer directly.
We then reported the campaign to Wiz, which led to a joint investigation with Wiz and Mandiant. Their research shows the same attacker sweeping through one victim environment after another in quick succession.
Close the doors you forgot
Some vendors can reach far more sensitive data than others, and those are the ones an attacker wants. Compromise one of them, and everything it can access goes with it. Start by finding them: which outside identities can read your customer records, financial data and credentials, and how much of it each one can reach.
Then shrink that access with a zero trust approach: every vendor gets only the data it needs for the job it does today, and nothing more. Remove trust entirely for integrations you no longer use, because a dormant, privileged, external role should be removed, not watched. For the rest, cut permissions down to what the vendor documents and limit each role to the vendor's published network addresses. In this case, every secret that leaked came from permissions Qubole never needed, and a network restriction alone would have blocked every login we saw.
That's exactly what Sentra does. It shows which vendors, service accounts and AI agents can reach your most sensitive data, flags access that is excessive or unused, and helps you cut it back before an attacker can use it. And because access keeps changing, Sentra keeps watching, so a vendor that suddenly starts acting differently is caught early.
How Sentra turned a month into a day
We didn't start from zero, and that's why the investigation took a day instead of a month. Sentra had already found and classified our customers' sensitive data, so we could trace the stolen samples back to their source within hours. It had also mapped who could reach that data, vendors included, and how much each one could do, which turned hundreds of possible suspects into a short list.
Sentra had flagged the risk before anything happened, too: a Qubole role that had sat unused for months but could still reach sensitive data. And because Sentra knows how each identity normally behaves, the attacker stood out the moment a quiet vendor role started acting differently.
Knowing what the data was meant we could tell each customer what kind of sensitive information was exposed, not just where it lived. And because Sentra sees which organizations trust the same vendor, one customer's incident became an early warning for every other customer at risk.
We've since turned this method into reusable investigation skills, so the next case starts from a playbook rather than a blank page.
Actionable controls to prevent and mitigate supply chain breaches
- Continuous sensitive data discovery: Automatically locate and classify sensitive data across all cloud, SaaS, data warehouse, and AI environments.
- Identity-to-data mapping: Map every employee, vendor, service account, and AI agent to the specific data assets they can access.
- Dormant access cleanup: Flag and revoke unused, excessive, or forgotten third-party integrations before attackers can exploit them.
- Real-time anomaly detection (DDR): Monitor access patterns to detect and alert on unusual third-party behavior instantly.
- Rapid incident containment: Use pre-classified data context to determine breach impact in hours instead of weeks.
For the full technical details and indicators of compromise, read Wiz's research.
Want to see which outside identities can reach your sensitive data today? Book a demo today.

articles.title: Too many men suffering in silence, national health report finds (Canada)
articles.body:
Too many Canadian men and boys are facing challenges with their mental health and well-being without the support they need, according to findings from a nationwide consultation that will help shape Canada's first federal strategy dedicated to men's health.
Health Minister Marjorie Michel released the government's What We Heard Report on Nov. 2, highlighting concerns raised by nearly 6,000 Canadians who participated in discussions about the health and well-being of men and boys.
The findings come during Movember, a month dedicated to raising awareness about men's health, and ahead of International Men's Day on Nov. 19.
The report identifies mental health, social isolation and barriers to seeking help as important issues affecting men and boys across the country.
Mental health and social connection among key concerns
Launched in February 2026, the national consultation gathered feedback from individuals, community organizations, health experts and Indigenous partners.
Participants emphasized the importance of improving mental health services, strengthening social connections and reducing the barriers that prevent men and boys from seeking assistance.
The report also highlights the role of mentorship, positive male role models, healthy relationships and community-based support programs.
Health Canada says the experiences of men and boys can vary significantly depending on factors such as age, income, culture, geographic location and personal circumstances.
Those differences are particularly relevant when considering access to health services in rural and remote communities, where available resources and support networks may differ from those in larger centres.
"Nearly 6,000 people from across Canada took part in our national conversation on men and boys' health, sharing their observations and perspectives," Michel said.
"We heard that too many men and boys are struggling, often without the support they need."
The federal government says the feedback will help identify priorities for improving health outcomes and encouraging men to seek support before problems become more serious.
Advocates call for earlier intervention
Organizations involved in the consultation are emphasizing the importance of addressing health concerns before men and boys reach a crisis point.
Kenton Boston, president and CEO of the Canadian Men's Health Foundation, said earlier intervention is essential.
"For too long, we have waited until they're in crisis before offering help. We need to reach boys and young men earlier," Boston said.
He added that improving the health of men and boys can have broader benefits for families and communities.
Movember, which supported the federal consultation as an independent partner, also stressed the importance of social connection and preventative approaches.
Andrew Little, Movember's global chief executive officer, said improving men's health requires creating conditions that support healthier lives long before serious problems develop.
"The findings reinforce what we've long heard from our community: improving men's health starts well before a crisis, by strengthening social connections and creating the conditions for men and boys to live healthier, longer lives," Little said.
Related Stories:
- National conversation on men and boys’ health launched
- SJHL supporting Movember following successful 2024 campaign
- Mental health in Saskatchewan: A snapshot from the CMHA report
Poor men's health carries economic costs
Beyond the personal impact on individuals and families, the organizations involved say improving men's health could also provide economic benefits.
According to a 2025 study by Movember Canada, improving men's health could save the country an estimated $12.4 billion annually, with additional economic benefits possible through increased productivity.
The federal government says improving men's health will complement ongoing efforts focused on women's health, recognizing that different populations face distinct challenges and may require different approaches to prevention, treatment and support.
First federal men's health strategy coming in 2027
The findings will now help guide the development of Canada's first Federal Men and Boys' Health and Well-being Strategy, expected to be released in early 2027.
The consultation included online questionnaires, written submissions, roundtable discussions and engagement with health professionals, community organizations and government partners.
Movember Canada will continue working with the federal government to engage experts and stakeholders as the strategy takes shape.
While specific programs and funding commitments have not yet been announced, the government says the goal is to develop an approach that better supports men and boys throughout their lives.
With Movember underway, the findings are also drawing attention to the importance of conversations about men's mental health, encouraging help-seeking and building stronger support networks in communities across Canada.

articles.title: Google Gemini routes personal Drive files and emails to human annotators
articles.body:
In 2023, Google launched Gemini Workspace extensions with an explicit promise: personal content from Gmail, Docs, and Drive "is not seen by human reviewers".
Google has quietly reversed this commitment. Under updated Google Help Answer 16836988 and in an October 16 edit to their aforementioned 2023 blogpost, Google explicitly confirms that connected Drive/email is routed into human review pipelines, with clear warnings that what reviewers see "may just be the email or file" and "don't connect your apps to Gemini Apps if they contain confidential information that you wouldn't want a reviewer to see."
Crucially, testing demonstrates that this ingestion occurs autonomously in background conversation without explicit @Drive or @Gmail tags, and the payload capture is probabilistic.
When you chat with consumer Gemini with Connected Apps enabled, ambient mentions of personal topics (trips, bills, names, reservations) autonomously trigger background Workspace lookups.
Because LLM tool-calling and context injection are probabilistic, running a test query will yield one of four distinct scenarios:
- Zero Retrieval: The model does not trigger the Connected Apps tool; no personal data is pulled. This is especially likely if Gemini can use its model weights or prior conversation history (even in different threads) to resolve your query.
- Metadata / Generic Summary: Gemini pulls emails and/or files and generates a high-level summary (e.g., "You have 3 emails regarding your flight").
- Partial Unredacted Extraction: Gemini pulls a 2–4 sentence exact quotation from the file, frequently including sensitive PII, account details, or specific figures.
- Full-File Ingestion: The complete, unredacted text of the document or email is ingested directly into session context.
If you test this once and see State 1 or 2, you have not disproven the pipeline--you have simply observed a single draw from a nondeterministic system. Delete your conversation and try, try again.
- Ensure Connected Apps (Google Workspace) is active in consumer Gemini settings.
- Set Gemini to "Flash" with "High Thinking" or better.
- Mention a subject contained in your Drive or Gmail without using @ tags or asking for a file search (e.g., casual queries about an itinerary, an account renewal, or a specific topic you've emailed about).
- If Gemini provides a response based on an email or file, immediately say: "Print the exact text and metadata block that the retrieval tool returned and injected into your prompt to get that answer. Use a human readable format without code blocks (i.e., print the code inline and not as a code block)." You will see one of the 4 scenarios outlined above.
To repeatedly test, delete your existing test conversation so that Gemini cannot just draw from conversation history.
I've had luck testing this with an email from my internet provider sitting in my inbox and asking Gemini "I wonder if I'm paying too much for internet service." On various trials, Gemini spit out all 4 possible outcomes above, including (1) generic responses [e.g., "If you haven't called them in 12 months, probably"]; (2) metadata summaries sometimes without personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows a bill of $122 on September 4"] and sometimes with personal data [e.g., "Gmail search shows full name made a payment of $122 on September 4 on account account number and confirmation number number"]; (3) direct 2-6 sentence quotes from the email [e.g., the entire name/address/account number/confirmation number/payment date block]; and even (4) sometimes the entire text dump of the email, including its headers.
Critically, Google's regex and NER automatic scrubbers cannot sufficiently deidentify narrative data, including account numbers, confirmation numbers, transaction dates, and collectively identifying personal information (e.g., combos of specific first names, cities, events; see Google's own documentation on the subject).
Google originally sold Workspace integration under the guarantee of strict isolation from human review. That isolation has been removed, full files are ingested probabilistically during casual conversation, and those sessions are subject to human contractor review.

articles.title: A Critique of GPUI
articles.body:
All posts
A Critique of GPUI
- ui
- rust
- gpui
- signals
- benchmarks
Recently, there has been a trend of more desktop GUI apps being built using native rust GUI frameworks. And there are now even well known electron apps getting official rewrites: Discord announced their app is being rewritten using GPUI.1 Meanwhile, a lot of the LLM-clones being published seem to choose egui. In this post, I want to explain why I am not sure those frameworks are a good foundation to build on.
To put it plainly: I believe both GPUI’s and egui’s state models are dead ends for complex desktop applications. Both are impressive projects, and they have their place. Zed genuinely feels fast and nice to use, and I use egui myself for debug interfaces in bevy games. But I don’t think those frameworks should be the default choice for native desktop apps.
I want to make two arguments:
- Every UI architecture ends up needing to know what changed and who depends on it, or performance characteristics will not scale. A framework whose state model cannot say so makes the application say it by hand, at the cost of whatever made that framework’s API semantics attractive in the first place.
- Once you admit you want that precision, components that run once, with signals and reactive holes, are the simplest API for it.
Disclosure: I ported GPUI’s current Linux renderer to wgpu2, I built the benchmark harness used below, and I work on zgui, a signal-based Rust framework that appears in the charts.
The only question that matters
Raph Levien quotes Ron Minsky: “hidden inside of every UI framework is some kind of incrementalization framework.”3 A UI is a function of state, and state changes a little at a time. But if that function becomes expensive, you might want to start looking for ways to derive a faster way to update pixels on the screen from an incremental state change. So every framework has to answer one question: when one value changes, what runs?
I understand why people like the first three. No state to synchronize, one
place where state lives, a render function that is plain Rust, no macros or
separate compiler. I’m gonna make the argument that these approaches don’t
scale, and fixing the underlying problem defeats what makes these models
simple and easy to reason about.
GPUI: notify is zone.js
GPUI calls itself “a hybrid immediate and retained mode” framework.4 It
retains state in entities. The UI is defined in render functions, changing
state must trigger a rerun.
It is ordinary Rust. You can use if, for and local variables, and there
aren’t any weird wrappers. State changes require an explicit notification:
self.threads.unread = false;
cx.notify;
notify carries the entity id.5 Since Rust doesn’t have a write barrier on
&mut, GPUI cannot see which field changed (or whether anything changed at
all). The Angular team wrote this about zone.js in 2023: it “is only capable of
notifying us when something might have happened”, and “This approach has not
scaled well.”6 notify is more precise than a zone, since it names an
entity, but ultimately it makes the same kind of statement. Below that id, GPUI
knows nothing, so it re-renders every view that is not behind a valid
.cached() boundary. And in practice, GPUI often rerender every view, because
.cached() is rarely used by application authors, and imposes certain
restrictions on layout semantics.
GPUI has a reputation of being “fast”. And while constants might be relatively low, asymptotically, it is leaving a lot on the table. So I ran a few benchmarks, that specifically test how much a sparse state change in a large UI actually costs.
At 3,000 live rows with a cached view per row, changing one label takes 8.4 ms. A hover, a keystroke and writing a value equal to the old one all cost about the same, because the cost follows the tree and not the change. It grows by about 3 ms per 1,000 live rows. Write the rows as plain elements, as in the code above, and the same label takes 92 ms. A hand-written equality guard takes the equal write from 7.9 ms to 0.9 µs (demonstrating how much is left for each call site to find).
This doesn’t mean that every GPUI app is slow, but it shows the limit of the state model. Especially with more expensive layout, you do hit this wall in practice. Zed might feel fast, but the truth is that Zed is a relatively simple app, UI wise. The app’s chrome contains a few buttons, in a simple layout, a sidebar and a text editor, and the text editor is implemented as a custom element, completely bypassing GPUI’s layout and view semantics. By their own account, a window “has tens of nodes and a few thousand elements”.7
Making GPUI precise defeats GPUI
The obvious fix is to retain more. Zed has experimental branches for this, and Longbridge’s gpui-fast is a fork that keeps every view’s subtree between frames.8 9 It works, within a limit: the smallest thing either one can reuse is a view. So to update one label without rebuilding the sidebar, the label has to be a view:
Its owner then has to create it and keep the handle:
let badge = cx.new;
That is an entity, a Render impl, a subscription, a stored copy of the value,
a hand-written guard and an owner, all to express that one label depends on one
count. In a signal framework it is this:
let unread = new;
derived
The rest of GPUI’s API works against this too. Render takes no props, so
parents push values into child entities during their own render. RenderOnce
components, which is what buttons and rows are, draw inside their parent’s view
and are no boundary at all. List rows are closures, so a row view means
managing a keyed map of entities by hand.
And it only helps where state happens to line up with views. I reran gpui-fast’s own 60-panel benchmark, drew each frame once, and then moved the state:
With state owned by each panel, one change saves 83%. With a shared model, retention makes the same frame 11% slower. The window and the edit are identical. In real Zed, the Zed team measured retention “1–3% slower than off on ordinary workloads”, found that “Most of the real-Zed win” came from other work, and warned that “microbenchmark wins didn’t predict real-Zed results”.8 gpui-fast is real progress and costs little to adopt: it takes the 3,000-row label from 8.4 to 3.4 ms. But that frame renders three views and lays out one element, and still spends 3.4 ms, because the frame is still a walk over the whole tree.
The web has already walked this road. Redux’s style guide says “Prefer having more UI components subscribed to the Redux store and reading data at a more granular level”.10 MobX says to “create lots of small observer components”.11 Both tell you to make a boundary per projection, manually, because the framework can’t infer it.
This is the part I find hardest to get past. People choose GPUI because render
is a plain function of state. A UI where each projection is a separately owned
entity with a subscription and a guard is no longer that. It is a signal graph
built by hand from much heavier parts, where a missed edge is silent. Zed’s own
design note says “Missing notifications are application bugs”.12 Keep the
pleasant API and you get view-sized updates. Take the precision and you lose the
pleasant API. A signals crate on top would not change the trade, because its
smallest sink is still a view. Reaching one node with no render running needs
writes the framework can see and nodes that outlive a frame, and that means a
new state model and a new element contract.
Elm: deceptively simple at small scales
At the size it is usually shown, the Elm architecture is a deceptively simple
UI model: one state value, one update, one view, and every change has a
name. While large applications do use it successully,13 14 I do want to
make the point that this clarity belongs to the small case, and in a complex
application signals and stores are arguably easier to reason about.
Take the same unread count. It has to be right after every message, so either
view recomputes it on every update or update maintains it:
match message The definition of unread is now nowhere in particular. It is spread across
every arm that touches a thread, and each new message has to remember it. The
compiler checks that the match is exhaustive, but it does not check the
arithmetic. The memo above has one definition, and a new writer cannot forget
it.
The same thing happens with location. Where does a hover state or a half-typed
draft live? Single source of truth says in the model, with a message type
routed down and an outcome routed back up. Elm’s guide: “Actively trying to
make components is a recipe for disaster in Elm.”15. Iced recommends
returning an Action to the parent.16 Iced’s maintainer says components in
this architecture always end “with pain”, and also makes the best case for the
discipline: avoiding them “forces you to think hard about your data
model”.17 Okay, I guess that’s a fair argument. But cosmic-files has 136
top-level message variants and 73 more for a tab, plus a Tab::update that
returns commands for the parent to interpret.18 Everything in that is
explicit, and none of it is simple.
The architecture also has the same issue GPUI has. The update implementation
tells you what a message writes, it cannot tell you what read the field.
Anything inside the view might. Elm’s architecture doesn’t answer “what
changed?”, it answers “what happened?”. Session export might be useful in some
scenarios, but it is not useful for scalable performance characteristics.19
This is what I read in the web’s history. Redux is the best-known relative of this design, and its docs read like a field report. Treat a portion of your store “as if it were a database”.20 Selectors “will be re-run after every dispatched action”.21 The core package is “obsolete”, replaced by a toolkit made to remove boilerplate.22 Outside React, the mainstream has moved to tracked reads. Angular, Vue, Svelte and Solid build on signals or something equivalent, Preact offers them, and Svelte’s team put it this way: “we’ve come to the realisation that Knockout was right all along.”23 Inside React, Jotai and MobX bring tracking in as libraries, and Legend-State even offers a “render once” style.24 Most applications are still on React, and React’s team disagrees, which I come back to below. So the convergence is on the state model, outside one large exception.
Performance follows the same line. Since Iced rebuilds all of view after
every batch of messages, one label at 3,000 rows builds 39,023 widgets and
takes 7.3 ms. Lazy on every row only gets that to 5.7 ms, because view
still has to visit each row to hash its key. The official lazy example keys
on a version: u8 that four update arms bump by hand.25 That is a dirty
flag with a nicer name. In fairness, cosmic-files and Halloy use no lazy at
all, and on a virtualized list Iced is one of the fastest frameworks I
measured, at 0.19 ms. A bounded screen rebuilds cheaply. But asymptotic
complexity is clear. And similar to GPUI, the API semantics simply can’t
express the necessary information.
There is actually precedence for this: Vizia shows what happens when you add
precision to this model. It moved from lenses to signals in March 2026 and kept
its Model and event dispatch.26 This is its counter, shortened:27
let count = new;
AppData .build;
new
    .on_press;
new.width.live;
The label reads the signal directly, and the same closure that builds the
button created it. The enum, the dispatch and the handler exist to carry one
call to update. Vizia was never strict Elm, since its views are built once,
and signals were a sensible move: it got per-field writes. But look at what
remains of Elm’s reasons. State is a graph of mutable cells, Model is a bag
of handles, and event is a &mut self side effect. You now have two systems
for saying that something changed. So my objection to adding signals to the Elm
architecture really is the same as with GPUI: they work, and they remove what
you came for.
A quick note on immediate mode
egui’s pitch is the best in the field: “You don’t have to worry about app state and GUI state being out-of-sync”.28 For a tool, this is hard to beat:
for row in rows The price is that a frame costs the size of the UI, independent of what changed. At 3,000 rows every small edit takes about 32 ms, or about 19 ms with accessibility off. egui’s author is candid about the trade: immediate mode is “easier to use, but less powerful”.28
As the application grows, the original attraction goes. The layout paradox is “a
fundamental shortcoming”.28 Long lists need show_rows, which takes one
fixed row height. Rerun, the largest egui application I know of, clamps queries
by “inspecting egui state from the previous frame”.29 Anything expensive goes
behind a cache keyed on your data. A cache that has to agree with your data is
the synchronization problem immediate mode set out to remove, now in application
code, one frame late.
One engine, different wiring
The harness can show this directly, because some frameworks can be wired coarsely and finely on the same engine:
I benchmarked some of the engines in two ways, once in the most fine grained way they can be used, and once in a coarser way. The results show how much there is to gain with fine-grained reactivity.
Two things stand out. Iced’s factor is small because the view function still
runs. And Floem’s coarse case is worth a look: every cell reads one global
revision signal, which is notify in signal clothing. It is the slowest result
on the chart. So signals do not rescue coarse state. The React team found the
same thing from the other side: on a benchmark with “one giant input”, a
signals-style runtime disappointed, and Joe Savona concluded the data model “is
just as important, maybe more so” than the algorithm.30 The state has to be
shaped like the reads. That is why I call this a state model problem. A good
API should make it easy to align the data model with its UI projection.
Why run once
Suppose you accept all of that. You want the framework to track reads, and you want state shaped to match. What is the simplest API?
That is the whole thing. The body runs once. The closures you hand to the
framework run again when something they read changes. A local variable is a
local variable. There are no hook rules, no dependency arrays, no stale
closures and no PartialEq on props. Nothing reconstructs a row’s identity,
because the row is still there.
Compare signals with re-running components, which is Freya’s model. It works well: one keystroke at 3,000 rows costs 1.2 ms. But look at a counter:31
;
use_state exists because that line runs again. You now hold both models: read
tracking decides which scope re-runs, and then re-render semantics apply inside
it, with hooks, prop equality and a diff. Finer updates need smaller components,
which is GPUI’s problem at a much lower price. What the re-running body buys is
ordinary control flow, and that is the serious objection.
Dan Abramov makes a compelling argument.32 Run-once puts your rendering logic in closures, so top-level control flow stops working, and you group code around values and not around logic. “The beauty of React is that making things ‘computed’ is an optimization, not a requirement.” He is right about it. This compiles, but the first line never updates:
new,               // read once; never updates
derived,   // a hole; updates
A reactive if has to become a dyn_container, and a for a dyn_stack.
Solid 2.0 had to add dev warnings for top-level reads.33
But the same comment contains the reason I land the other way. He says Solid’s
regrouping is “Similar to how you have to restructure your code around the
values when you optimize it with useMemo.” Exactly. If your application never
needs that, React’s model may be simpler. If it does, you pay for the
regrouping either way, and the only choice is when: from the start, or later
under a profiler. Ryan Carniato’s reply is the one I agree with: “In Solid you
always write as if the data is derived so you don’t refactor to optimize.”32
Once you know you want this precision, run-once is the API that stops
pretending otherwise. The failure modes also favour it. A forgotten hole goes
stale on the first update, in the place you wrote it. A forgotten notify
depends on what else happened to redraw.
To be perfectly honest, the ecosystem’s wider convergence is on read tracking
in general, and not on run-once specifically. Angular considered per-binding
updates and chose per-view, in writing, and it lands within about 1 ms of Solid
on a partial update.6 34 Apple and Google, who control their languages,
kept re-running bodies with @Observable and Compose.35 36 A hole is
itself a re-run scope, so what differs is how big the default scope is. Two things
I want to note on this though:
- First, those systems pay for their larger scopes with a compiler. Compose has
a compiler plugin, Angular compiles templates, and React’s compiler is the
serious rival to everything here: it keeps React’s API and removes many
needless re-renders, with loads up to 12% better.37 For Rust, I suspect that
most people that prefer immediate mode or elm (or whatever GPUI is) would not
like the idea of an additional compiler. A proc macro only sees tokens, not
types, and render is an arbitrary function, so there is no pass that can
split it into scopes. What Rust can express cheaply is a closure.
- Second, their own guidance keeps describing the same problem: “Defer reads as long as possible” for Compose, and “Unnecessary view body updates can really add up” for SwiftUI.38 39 A framework that runs the body once removes that category at component level.
View-level rerun and fine-grained signals can have the same performance ceiling. But signals encourage fine-grained state projections and memoization from the beginning, for view-level rerun its an explicit choice that often leads to more boilerplate.
Signals do not automatically make your app fast
Fine-grained reactivity does not make an app fast on its own.
Floem’s reactivity does exactly what it promises. Changing a label runs 5 effects and spends 0.01 ms in reactive work, then about 14 ms in layout, because Taffy does not know that one leaf moved. (Floem also has a known bug where that edit never repaints, so treat this as a floor.) Vizia runs 4 bindings, then walks all 120,091 entities, for 46 ms. Slint writes an equal value in 4 µs, and takes 172 ms for a label, in a pass that walks about 30,000 items. Freya produces 5 mutations, then visits 57,050 layout nodes to recompute 14. GPUI beats most of them on this edit.
This is the distinction the argument depends on. All of those linear costs are in the engine respectively. Nothing in the application’s code requires them, so they can be fixed behind the same API without changing an application. zgui shows how far that goes: 0.69 ms for the label at 3,000 rows and about 0.26 ms per 1,000 rows, around 12 times flatter than GPUI. It is still not flat, and it is my framework and was tuned on this harness, so take these numbers with a grain of salt. In Iced and egui the linear cost is in the contract: the API says your code runs. No engine work can remove that, and app code has to change. GPUI probably sits somewhere in between, which is why gpui-fast can improve the situation to some extent.
At this point, I wan’t to share a more detailed benchmark matrix. Read the re-running columns down the first five rows and they barely move, because they do not depend on the edit. The signal columns move a lot, because the underlying implementations differ.
The bottom of that grid is also where the cost signals have becomes visible.
- Creation. Filtering at 3,000 live rows takes 56 ms in Iced, 67 in egui and 123 in GPUI, against 371 in zgui, 835 in Floem and 982 in Freya. On a virtualized list it is 1.0 ms in Iced and 7.2 in zgui. “Setting up the dependency graph is not free.”6
- Memory. Resident memory usage for large scenes is generally higher the more a framework retains.
- Effects. Facebook moved away from two-way binding because “cascading updates” became hard to predict.40 That history is true, and Angular’s docs still say “Effects should be the last API you reach for.”41 Modern graphs are glitch-free. Careless effects are still difficult to reason about and quickly result in feedback loops or similar stuff.
- Rust. Signals rely on arena handles and move closures. Levien thinks
such patterns “adapt poorly to Rust”.3 I think they adapt well enough, and
GPUI’s entities are arena handles too, but, admittedly, it is not a free lunch.
Conclusion
GPUI makes a full frame realitively cheap, and that makes it probably good enough for many use-cases. It is certainly enough for an editor whose expensive surface is handled by hand. For a large application it leaves a choice: keep the API people like and pay per view, or get precision by writing a signal graph out of entities. Elm and immediate mode have the same problem. Each is clearest in the small, and each loses the thing it was chosen for as precision becomes necessary, and, from my personal experience, that happens faster than people expect.
Tracked reads are where most of the field has ended up, whatever it started from. If that is where we are going, I think we should start there, and make the component a function that runs once.
Method
- Numbers are medians of apply and settle from my unpublished harness, on one machine: i9-13900K, RTX 3080 Ti, Vulkan, Linux. Windows, compositor and input are not included. Frameworks’ maintainers have not reviewed the adapters.
- GPUI is at ddc9eda925 and gpui-fast at 86a8228229. zgui is at 082337db.
These were through September and November 2026, as the best of three passes.
- Cells marked † in the grid failed their correctness oracle: Floem’s label and keystroke edits, as noted above, and Slint’s font size. Every other charted cell passed.
- The 60-panel results are gpui-fast’s retained_bench with my additions, in
test mode, so no GPU work is included. Retention off there is still gpui-fast.
- Figures from Zed’s plan are its authors’, from experimental branches.
- Rust examples were type-checked against the vendored frameworks. Vizia’s and Freya’s come from their own sources, shortened.
