GPUI has a reputation of being “fast”. And while constants might be relatively low, asymptotically, it is leaving a lot on the table. So I ran a few benchmarks, that specifically test how much a sparse state change in a large UI actually costs.
At 3,000 live rows with a cached view per row, changing one label takes 8.4 ms. A hover, a keystroke and writing a value equal to the old one all cost about the same, because the cost follows the tree and not the change. It grows by about 3 ms per 1,000 live rows. Write the rows as plain elements, as in the code above, and the same label takes 92 ms. A hand-written equality guard takes the equal write from 7.9 ms to 0.9 µs (demonstrating how much is left for each call site to find).
This doesn’t mean that every GPUI app is slow, but it shows the limit of the state model. Especially with more expensive layout, you do hit this wall in practice. Zed might feel fast, but the truth is that Zed is a relatively simple app, UI wise. The app’s chrome contains a few buttons, in a simple layout, a sidebar and a text editor, and the text editor is implemented as a custom element, completely bypassing GPUI’s layout and view semantics. By their own account, a window “has tens of nodes and a few thousand elements”.7
Making GPUI precise defeats GPUI
The obvious fix is to retain more. Zed has experimental branches for this, and Longbridge’s gpui-fast is a fork that keeps every view’s subtree between frames.8 9 It works, within a limit: the smallest thing either one can reuse is a view. So to update one label without rebuilding the sidebar, the label has to be a view:
Its owner then has to create it and keep the handle:
let badge = cx.new;
That is an entity, a Render impl, a subscription, a stored copy of the value,
a hand-written guard and an owner, all to express that one label depends on one
count. In a signal framework it is this:
let unread = new;
derived
The rest of GPUI’s API works against this too. Render takes no props, so
parents push values into child entities during their own render. RenderOnce
components, which is what buttons and rows are, draw inside their parent’s view
and are no boundary at all. List rows are closures, so a row view means
managing a keyed map of entities by hand.
And it only helps where state happens to line up with views. I reran gpui-fast’s own 60-panel benchmark, drew each frame once, and then moved the state:
With state owned by each panel, one change saves 83%. With a shared model, retention makes the same frame 11% slower. The window and the edit are identical. In real Zed, the Zed team measured retention “1–3% slower than off on ordinary workloads”, found that “Most of the real-Zed win” came from other work, and warned that “microbenchmark wins didn’t predict real-Zed results”.8 gpui-fast is real progress and costs little to adopt: it takes the 3,000-row label from 8.4 to 3.4 ms. But that frame renders three views and lays out one element, and still spends 3.4 ms, because the frame is still a walk over the whole tree.
The web has already walked this road. Redux’s style guide says “Prefer having more UI components subscribed to the Redux store and reading data at a more granular level”.10 MobX says to “create lots of small observer components”.11 Both tell you to make a boundary per projection, manually, because the framework can’t infer it.
This is the part I find hardest to get past. People choose GPUI because render
is a plain function of state. A UI where each projection is a separately owned
entity with a subscription and a guard is no longer that. It is a signal graph
built by hand from much heavier parts, where a missed edge is silent. Zed’s own
design note says “Missing notifications are application bugs”.12 Keep the
pleasant API and you get view-sized updates. Take the precision and you lose the
pleasant API. A signals crate on top would not change the trade, because its
smallest sink is still a view. Reaching one node with no render running needs
writes the framework can see and nodes that outlive a frame, and that means a
new state model and a new element contract.
Elm: deceptively simple at small scales
At the size it is usually shown, the Elm architecture is a deceptively simple
UI model: one state value, one update, one view, and every change has a
name. While large applications do use it successully,13 14 I do want to
make the point that this clarity belongs to the small case, and in a complex
application signals and stores are arguably easier to reason about.
Take the same unread count. It has to be right after every message, so either
view recomputes it on every update or update maintains it:
match message The definition of unread is now nowhere in particular. It is spread across
every arm that touches a thread, and each new message has to remember it. The
compiler checks that the match is exhaustive, but it does not check the
arithmetic. The memo above has one definition, and a new writer cannot forget
it.
The same thing happens with location. Where does a hover state or a half-typed
draft live? Single source of truth says in the model, with a message type
routed down and an outcome routed back up. Elm’s guide: “Actively trying to
make components is a recipe for disaster in Elm.”15. Iced recommends
returning an Action to the parent.16 Iced’s maintainer says components in
this architecture always end “with pain”, and also makes the best case for the
discipline: avoiding them “forces you to think hard about your data
model”.17 Okay, I guess that’s a fair argument. But cosmic-files has 136
top-level message variants and 73 more for a tab, plus a Tab::update that
returns commands for the parent to interpret.18 Everything in that is
explicit, and none of it is simple.
The architecture also has the same issue GPUI has. The update implementation
tells you what a message writes, it cannot tell you what read the field.
Anything inside the view might. Elm’s architecture doesn’t answer “what
changed?”, it answers “what happened?”. Session export might be useful in some
scenarios, but it is not useful for scalable performance characteristics.19
This is what I read in the web’s history. Redux is the best-known relative of this design, and its docs read like a field report. Treat a portion of your store “as if it were a database”.20 Selectors “will be re-run after every dispatched action”.21 The core package is “obsolete”, replaced by a toolkit made to remove boilerplate.22 Outside React, the mainstream has moved to tracked reads. Angular, Vue, Svelte and Solid build on signals or something equivalent, Preact offers them, and Svelte’s team put it this way: “we’ve come to the realisation that Knockout was right all along.”23 Inside React, Jotai and MobX bring tracking in as libraries, and Legend-State even offers a “render once” style.24 Most applications are still on React, and React’s team disagrees, which I come back to below. So the convergence is on the state model, outside one large exception.
Performance follows the same line. Since Iced rebuilds all of view after
every batch of messages, one label at 3,000 rows builds 39,023 widgets and
takes 7.3 ms. Lazy on every row only gets that to 5.7 ms, because view
still has to visit each row to hash its key. The official lazy example keys
on a version: u8 that four update arms bump by hand.25 That is a dirty
flag with a nicer name. In fairness, cosmic-files and Halloy use no lazy at
all, and on a virtualized list Iced is one of the fastest frameworks I
measured, at 0.19 ms. A bounded screen rebuilds cheaply. But asymptotic
complexity is clear. And similar to GPUI, the API semantics simply can’t
express the necessary information.
There is actually precedence for this: Vizia shows what happens when you add
precision to this model. It moved from lenses to signals in March 2026 and kept
its Model and event dispatch.26 This is its counter, shortened:27
let count = new;
AppData .build;
new
    .on_press;
new.width.live;
The label reads the signal directly, and the same closure that builds the
button created it. The enum, the dispatch and the handler exist to carry one
call to update. Vizia was never strict Elm, since its views are built once,
and signals were a sensible move: it got per-field writes. But look at what
remains of Elm’s reasons. State is a graph of mutable cells, Model is a bag
of handles, and event is a &mut self side effect. You now have two systems
for saying that something changed. So my objection to adding signals to the Elm
architecture really is the same as with GPUI: they work, and they remove what
you came for.
A quick note on immediate mode
egui’s pitch is the best in the field: “You don’t have to worry about app state and GUI state being out-of-sync”.28 For a tool, this is hard to beat:
for row in rows The price is that a frame costs the size of the UI, independent of what changed. At 3,000 rows every small edit takes about 32 ms, or about 19 ms with accessibility off. egui’s author is candid about the trade: immediate mode is “easier to use, but less powerful”.28
As the application grows, the original attraction goes. The layout paradox is “a
fundamental shortcoming”.28 Long lists need show_rows, which takes one
fixed row height. Rerun, the largest egui application I know of, clamps queries
by “inspecting egui state from the previous frame”.29 Anything expensive goes
behind a cache keyed on your data. A cache that has to agree with your data is
the synchronization problem immediate mode set out to remove, now in application
code, one frame late.
One engine, different wiring
The harness can show this directly, because some frameworks can be wired coarsely and finely on the same engine:
I benchmarked some of the engines in two ways, once in the most fine grained way they can be used, and once in a coarser way. The results show how much there is to gain with fine-grained reactivity.
Two things stand out. Iced’s factor is small because the view function still
runs. And Floem’s coarse case is worth a look: every cell reads one global
revision signal, which is notify in signal clothing. It is the slowest result
on the chart. So signals do not rescue coarse state. The React team found the
same thing from the other side: on a benchmark with “one giant input”, a
signals-style runtime disappointed, and Joe Savona concluded the data model “is
just as important, maybe more so” than the algorithm.30 The state has to be
shaped like the reads. That is why I call this a state model problem. A good
API should make it easy to align the data model with its UI projection.
Why run once
Suppose you accept all of that. You want the framework to track reads, and you want state shaped to match. What is the simplest API?
That is the whole thing. The body runs once. The closures you hand to the
framework run again when something they read changes. A local variable is a
local variable. There are no hook rules, no dependency arrays, no stale
closures and no PartialEq on props. Nothing reconstructs a row’s identity,
because the row is still there.
Compare signals with re-running components, which is Freya’s model. It works well: one keystroke at 3,000 rows costs 1.2 ms. But look at a counter:31
;
use_state exists because that line runs again. You now hold both models: read
tracking decides which scope re-runs, and then re-render semantics apply inside
it, with hooks, prop equality and a diff. Finer updates need smaller components,
which is GPUI’s problem at a much lower price. What the re-running body buys is
ordinary control flow, and that is the serious objection.
Dan Abramov makes a compelling argument.32 Run-once puts your rendering logic in closures, so top-level control flow stops working, and you group code around values and not around logic. “The beauty of React is that making things ‘computed’ is an optimization, not a requirement.” He is right about it. This compiles, but the first line never updates:
new,               // read once; never updates
derived,   // a hole; updates
A reactive if has to become a dyn_container, and a for a dyn_stack.
Solid 2.0 had to add dev warnings for top-level reads.33
But the same comment contains the reason I land the other way. He says Solid’s
regrouping is “Similar to how you have to restructure your code around the
values when you optimize it with useMemo.” Exactly. If your application never
needs that, React’s model may be simpler. If it does, you pay for the
regrouping either way, and the only choice is when: from the start, or later
under a profiler. Ryan Carniato’s reply is the one I agree with: “In Solid you
always write as if the data is derived so you don’t refactor to optimize.”32
Once you know you want this precision, run-once is the API that stops
pretending otherwise. The failure modes also favour it. A forgotten hole goes
stale on the first update, in the place you wrote it. A forgotten notify
depends on what else happened to redraw.
To be perfectly honest, the ecosystem’s wider convergence is on read tracking
in general, and not on run-once specifically. Angular considered per-binding
updates and chose per-view, in writing, and it lands within about 1 ms of Solid
on a partial update.6 34 Apple and Google, who control their languages,
kept re-running bodies with @Observable and Compose.35 36 A hole is
itself a re-run scope, so what differs is how big the default scope is. Two things
I want to note on this though:
- First, those systems pay for their larger scopes with a compiler. Compose has
a compiler plugin, Angular compiles templates, and React’s compiler is the
serious rival to everything here: it keeps React’s API and removes many
needless re-renders, with loads up to 12% better.37 For Rust, I suspect that
most people that prefer immediate mode or elm (or whatever GPUI is) would not
like the idea of an additional compiler. A proc macro only sees tokens, not
types, and render is an arbitrary function, so there is no pass that can
split it into scopes. What Rust can express cheaply is a closure.
- Second, their own guidance keeps describing the same problem: “Defer reads as long as possible” for Compose, and “Unnecessary view body updates can really add up” for SwiftUI.38 39 A framework that runs the body once removes that category at component level.
View-level rerun and fine-grained signals can have the same performance ceiling. But signals encourage fine-grained state projections and memoization from the beginning, for view-level rerun its an explicit choice that often leads to more boilerplate.
Signals do not automatically make your app fast
Fine-grained reactivity does not make an app fast on its own.
Floem’s reactivity does exactly what it promises. Changing a label runs 5 effects and spends 0.01 ms in reactive work, then about 14 ms in layout, because Taffy does not know that one leaf moved. (Floem also has a known bug where that edit never repaints, so treat this as a floor.) Vizia runs 4 bindings, then walks all 120,091 entities, for 46 ms. Slint writes an equal value in 4 µs, and takes 172 ms for a label, in a pass that walks about 30,000 items. Freya produces 5 mutations, then visits 57,050 layout nodes to recompute 14. GPUI beats most of them on this edit.
This is the distinction the argument depends on. All of those linear costs are in the engine respectively. Nothing in the application’s code requires them, so they can be fixed behind the same API without changing an application. zgui shows how far that goes: 0.69 ms for the label at 3,000 rows and about 0.26 ms per 1,000 rows, around 12 times flatter than GPUI. It is still not flat, and it is my framework and was tuned on this harness, so take these numbers with a grain of salt. In Iced and egui the linear cost is in the contract: the API says your code runs. No engine work can remove that, and app code has to change. GPUI probably sits somewhere in between, which is why gpui-fast can improve the situation to some extent.
At this point, I wan’t to share a more detailed benchmark matrix. Read the re-running columns down the first five rows and they barely move, because they do not depend on the edit. The signal columns move a lot, because the underlying implementations differ.
The bottom of that grid is also where the cost signals have becomes visible.
- Creation. Filtering at 3,000 live rows takes 56 ms in Iced, 67 in egui and 123 in GPUI, against 371 in zgui, 835 in Floem and 982 in Freya. On a virtualized list it is 1.0 ms in Iced and 7.2 in zgui. “Setting up the dependency graph is not free.”6
- Memory. Resident memory usage for large scenes is generally higher the more a framework retains.
- Effects. Facebook moved away from two-way binding because “cascading updates” became hard to predict.40 That history is true, and Angular’s docs still say “Effects should be the last API you reach for.”41 Modern graphs are glitch-free. Careless effects are still difficult to reason about and quickly result in feedback loops or similar stuff.
- Rust. Signals rely on arena handles and move closures. Levien thinks
such patterns “adapt poorly to Rust”.3 I think they adapt well enough, and
GPUI’s entities are arena handles too, but, admittedly, it is not a free lunch.
Conclusion
GPUI makes a full frame realitively cheap, and that makes it probably good enough for many use-cases. It is certainly enough for an editor whose expensive surface is handled by hand. For a large application it leaves a choice: keep the API people like and pay per view, or get precision by writing a signal graph out of entities. Elm and immediate mode have the same problem. Each is clearest in the small, and each loses the thing it was chosen for as precision becomes necessary, and, from my personal experience, that happens faster than people expect.
Tracked reads are where most of the field has ended up, whatever it started from. If that is where we are going, I think we should start there, and make the component a function that runs once.
Method
- Numbers are medians of apply and settle from my unpublished harness, on one machine: i9-13900K, RTX 3080 Ti, Vulkan, Linux. Windows, compositor and input are not included. Frameworks’ maintainers have not reviewed the adapters.
- GPUI is at ddc9eda925 and gpui-fast at 86a8228229. zgui is at 082337db.
These were through September and November 2026, as the best of three passes.
- Cells marked † in the grid failed their correctness oracle: Floem’s label and keystroke edits, as noted above, and Slint’s font size. Every other charted cell passed.
- The 60-panel results are gpui-fast’s retained_bench with my additions, in
test mode, so no GPU work is included. Retention off there is still gpui-fast.
- Figures from Zed’s plan are its authors’, from experimental branches.
- Rust examples were type-checked against the vendored frameworks. Vizia’s and Freya’s come from their own sources, shortened.

articles.title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
articles.body:
I'm Not Convinced The AI Bubble Exists
Posted on Sun 08 November 2026 in AI
The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth.
Expenses Are Sky-High, But Constrained
To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far. It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion, bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place. The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.
Outside of these expenses, AI doesn't cost that much to run. We don't have the full numbers for the entire industry here, but Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable. Crucially, the S-1 filing indicates that Anthropic has started to make more than their compute and infrastructure investments combined, which cuts against the idea that the cost of building data centres is inherently unsustainable. In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.
The only serious long-term expenses to contend with here is the massive amount of debt that's been taken out to pay for these data centres in the first place. Like I said before, it's hard to really figure out these commitments because of the complex way that they're issued, but we can do some back of the envelope math. If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars. Because this is very rough math, the total needed revenue might come in to well over 250 billion dollars a year, but the point stands. Even though this is an enormous expense, paying it off isn't unthinkable with the data we have so far. Some of the debt is in convertible notes as well, which can be repaid through shares instead of cash. In the first 6 months of 2026, Anthropic has recorded 72 billion dollars of loss in the form of shares that are due to lenders. The cost is only so high because the valuation has skyrocketed to an estimated 1 trillion dollars, which means that Anthropic has more than enough equity to make lenders whole.
Profits Can Grow, By A Lot
In their S-1 filing, Anthropic records their revenue going from 41 million in 2023, 386 million in 2024, 4.585 billion in 2025, and 16.3 billion in the first 6 months of 2026. That's an insane increase in revenue, and it's safe to assume that other major AI companies like OpenAI are also seeing similar increases as well. At some point, the rate of increase has to level off, but that doesn't have to happen anytime soon. When I look at the current capacity of AI, it really feels like there's so much potential for frontier models to be used that just aren't being applied yet. Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well. AI can't replace lawyers and doctors, but they can automate their paperwork and free up time for them to do other things. Outside of generative AI, self-driving cars are becoming a reality, with some evidence to suggest that they're even better than human drivers. AI adoption takes time, but there's no reason to think that AI usage isn't going to massively skyrocket, even if AI doesn't get any better than it is today (and it certainly will get better). In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from.
There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. You can't really have it both ways here. It's completely valid to be afraid of AI taking your job, but money is going to change hands when that happens. I don't know exactly what the future will look like or how long it'll take for mass AI adoption to really happen, but when I imagine how AI will change the world, it's hard for me to see AI consumption not being 10x what it is now.
Google Has No Moat, But Neither Does McDonald's
In 2023, a memo from Google called "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI" was leaked, which outlined how the open source community was keeping pace with AI labs. More broadly, the memo rejected the idea that any company can really have a durable advantage when it comes to AI development. It would certainly be profitable if they could, but there's already so much information and research out there that nobody can ever hope for their frontier models to stay on the frontier for long. That means that there will never be a point where a company wins the AI wars, just nonstop fighting as each company in the industry tries to one-up the others. You know what other company didn't have a moat and found itself in a war to sell a product that its competitors could easily copy? Popeyes during the chicken sandwich war. I know that sounds goofy, but from a business perspective, it's remarkably similar. None of the restaurants involved in the chicken sandwich war had an enduring competitive advantage over any of the others, and all of them had to deal with potential customers choosing to just cook at home instead, but it was still highly profitable for everybody involved. Simply saying that a company doesn't have a moat isn't enough to say that the company can't make money.
In theory, an AI company has to be worried about their users switching over to a competitor or using an open source model instead. In practice, this isn't a major concern. For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever. I know that it's a common hobby in tech circles, but normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something that's going to perform at most the exact same as ChatGPT. That means that in principle, there's only going to be a few models that the vast majority of people will ever use. People can theoretically switch from model to model, but people tend to settle in with a product and develop brand loyalty. For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used. This partially offsets the risk of losing customers to a different product. Another way that companies can make money without having a moat is through institutional lock-in. Once a large corporation has integrated a particular AI into their day to day operation, transitioning away isn't costless. They may even have contracts agreeing to buy a certain amount of tokens, which binds them to keep using the AI instead of transitioning.
There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise
A potential way for a bubble to pop is for the companies involved to run out of capital to spend while they grow, causing them to fail. With the enormous amount of churn and debt that AI companies have, this is a serious risk to consider. Even so, I think that it's premature to worry about these companies failing to raise capital when most of them haven't even had an IPO yet. When SpaceX (which is partially an AI company, despite the name) went public, they raised more than 80 billion dollars. Besides that, many AI companies haven't issued public debt yet, which is a major way to get loans if private lenders decide that they don't want to put more of their capital into AI. The ones that have issued public debt, like Alphabet and Meta, have excellent bond ratings. If they need more capital, they won't struggle to find people to give them a loan.
Of course, investors aren't the only way to get capital. Once AI companies become profitable (as they already seem to be), they can use those profits to fund growth and pay off debts. The idea that AI companies are forced to constantly look for new investors to keep their doors open is probably a few months antiquated. From how it looks from Anthropic's S-1, the AI world may be past the horizon when it came to taking risky bets and can now focus on reaping the rewards.
The AI Industry Doesn't Look Like Any Bubble We've Seen Before
When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations, which makes the burst obvious in hindsight. With public AI companies, we don't see that happening. Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years, but all of them have stable P/E ratios in their 20s. If the increase in their valuations were irrational (or even just in expectation of future growth as opposed to current earnings), you would expect the P/E ratios to go up. Instead, their valuations look exactly what we would expect from a healthy trillion dollar company. When the dot-com bubble happened, it was largely driven by companies that couldn't turn a profit or had P/E ratios in the hundreds. I'm not going to pretend that I'm an expert on financial bubbles, but I've never heard of a bubble where the companies involved had such a modest valuation based on their earnings, even if their earnings (and therefore their evaluations) are enormous.
A potential way that this could be a bubble is if AI proves to be a fad. A lot of this rise in valuations has been because of increased demand for GPUs and data centre utilization, which is downstream of the demand for AI. We might imagine that the AI labs are propped up by an enormous amount of invested capital, and this capital ends up propping up the valuations for companies that make or rent out GPUs. However, this doesn't seem to be happening. Alphabet has a full-stack AI supply chain, where they create ASICs for AI, train their own AI, integrate AI into their products, and rent out compute to customers. Their prospectus helpfully divides their revenue streams into Google Cloud for their rented compute and Google Services, which makes it easy to tell if Alphabet's increased earnings are mostly because of their data centres. The answer is no. Google Cloud revenue is growing more in terms of percentage, but Google Services is growing far more in absolute terms. Specifically, Google Services revenue grew by 37.8 billion dollars for a 12% increase, while Google Cloud revenue grew by 15.5 billion dollars for a 36% increase. Alphabet is definitely benefiting from renting out their data centres, but it's not the main reason why their earnings have skyrocketed. Meta doesn't rent out their data centres at all, but their prospectus also records them having massive increases in their revenue, on the order of an extra 30 billion dollars from 2024 to 2025, and another extra 30 billion from 2023 to 2024. This isn't foolhardy investors throwing money at any company that makes AI, this is real profit from companies that have found ways to monetize AI. Anthropic also seems to be experiencing an exponential growth in their revenue as well, based on their S-1 filing. The only real unknown is OpenAI, which purchases an enormous amount of compute from other companies. It's possible that their finances are terrible, but even if they go under, I'm not convinced that this amounts to a bubble bursting. If anything, it seems more likely that their competitors will just consolidate and fight for more of a market share instead of the collapse triggering a chain reaction that takes the industry down with it.
Conclusion
I didn't write this article as some big takedown of the AI bubble theory. Even with this evidence, there are serious risks to the financial sustainability of the AI industry. Public backlash against data centres are going to make it harder for the infrastructure necessary for the AI revolution to continue, and regulatory barriers may make it harder to develop or deploy new models. Besides that, there's an enormous risk of an autonomous AI hacker causing serious damage, causing public demand for AI to plummet. Also, even after writing out it's possible for AI companies to pay off their debt, I'm still concerned by how much it actually is. It's not good that they're using increasingly complex ways to fund their infrastructure investments, and this gamble can backfire if revenue growth suddenly slows down, which it certainly might. Don't YOLO your life savings on the AI revolution, or at least don't blame me if you lose the shirt off of your back. The reason I wrote this article is because I felt that discussion about AI has become something of an echo chamber, which is never a good way to figure out what's right or wrong. Despite the echo chamber, people's stated beliefs and actual behaviour are wildly divergent. It's one thing to say that AI is a bubble that's going to burst, but where is this investor money coming from if we're all in agreement here? At the end of the day, when people have to put their money where their mouth is, they pull it out of their mouth and use it to buy NVIDIA. They might be wrong to do so, but maybe they're not. Time will tell.
As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be. People are afraid of what's going to happen with AI, and rightfully so. Beyond fear for the future, AI in the present has become uncomfortably common, with AI slop everywhere online and increasingly even IRL. This has all happened so fast, it's easy to forget that ChatGPT came out a little less than 4 years ago. Our world has changed in such a scary and odd way, and while I have a pretty optimistic view of AI overall, I get why people would want it all to go away. So, people wishcast. They tell themselves that this is all a giant bubble, and one day soon, everything will crash down and immediately go back to how it used to be. For better or worse, that's not going to happen. Even if AI turns out to be a bubble, it will be a bubble in the same way that the internet was a bubble, where the underlying technology remains useful. We're only ever going to live in the AI era from this point on, and whatever happens as a result of that, hopefully it will at least be good for the economy.

articles.title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
articles.body:
I'm Not Convinced The AI Bubble Exists
Posted on Sun 08 November 2026 in AI
The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though. Nobody can see the future, but I think that there's a pretty realistic chance that the meteoritic growth of AI companies in the past few years is justified, and that they have even more room for growth.
Expenses Are Sky-High, But Constrained
To say that AI companies are spending an absurd amount of money is an understatement. The debt and spending commitments for AI companies are handled through complex vehicles that make it difficult to tell exactly how much their expenses actually are (a serious problem, and one of the most salient points in favour of AI being a bubble), but they've committed to spending at least 3 trillion dollars so far. It's also been estimated that AI companies have already spent 1.9 trillion, bringing the overall expense of the AI industry to around 5 trillion dollars. This is unprecedented levels of investment, and AI just can't be profitable if this level of spending is maintained. However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place. The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.
Outside of these expenses, AI doesn't cost that much to run. We don't have the full numbers for the entire industry here, but Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable. Crucially, the S-1 filing indicates that Anthropic has started to make more than their compute and infrastructure investments combined, which cuts against the idea that the cost of building data centres is inherently unsustainable. In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.
The only serious long-term expenses to contend with here is the massive amount of debt that's been taken out to pay for these data centres in the first place. Like I said before, it's hard to really figure out these commitments because of the complex way that they're issued, but we can do some back of the envelope math. If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars. Because this is very rough math, the total needed revenue might come in to well over 250 billion dollars a year, but the point stands. Even though this is an enormous expense, paying it off isn't unthinkable with the data we have so far. Some of the debt is in convertible notes as well, which can be repaid through shares instead of cash. In the first 6 months of 2026, Anthropic has recorded 72 billion dollars of loss in the form of shares that are due to lenders. The cost is only so high because the valuation has skyrocketed to an estimated 1 trillion dollars, which means that Anthropic has more than enough equity to make lenders whole.
Profits Can Grow, By A Lot
In their S-1 filing, Anthropic records their revenue going from 41 million in 2023, 386 million in 2024, 4.585 billion in 2025, and 16.3 billion in the first 6 months of 2026. That's an insane increase in revenue, and it's safe to assume that other major AI companies like OpenAI are also seeing similar increases as well. At some point, the rate of increase has to level off, but that doesn't have to happen anytime soon. When I look at the current capacity of AI, it really feels like there's so much potential for frontier models to be used that just aren't being applied yet. Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well. AI can't replace lawyers and doctors, but they can automate their paperwork and free up time for them to do other things. Outside of generative AI, self-driving cars are becoming a reality, with some evidence to suggest that they're even better than human drivers. AI adoption takes time, but there's no reason to think that AI usage isn't going to massively skyrocket, even if AI doesn't get any better than it is today (and it certainly will get better). In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from.
There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. You can't really have it both ways here. It's completely valid to be afraid of AI taking your job, but money is going to change hands when that happens. I don't know exactly what the future will look like or how long it'll take for mass AI adoption to really happen, but when I imagine how AI will change the world, it's hard for me to see AI consumption not being 10x what it is now.
Google Has No Moat, But Neither Does McDonald's
In 2023, a memo from Google called "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI" was leaked, which outlined how the open source community was keeping pace with AI labs. More broadly, the memo rejected the idea that any company can really have a durable advantage when it comes to AI development. It would certainly be profitable if they could, but there's already so much information and research out there that nobody can ever hope for their frontier models to stay on the frontier for long. That means that there will never be a point where a company wins the AI wars, just nonstop fighting as each company in the industry tries to one-up the others. You know what other company didn't have a moat and found itself in a war to sell a product that its competitors could easily copy? Popeyes during the chicken sandwich war. I know that sounds goofy, but from a business perspective, it's remarkably similar. None of the restaurants involved in the chicken sandwich war had an enduring competitive advantage over any of the others, and all of them had to deal with potential customers choosing to just cook at home instead, but it was still highly profitable for everybody involved. Simply saying that a company doesn't have a moat isn't enough to say that the company can't make money.
In theory, an AI company has to be worried about their users switching over to a competitor or using an open source model instead. In practice, this isn't a major concern. For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever. I know that it's a common hobby in tech circles, but normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something that's going to perform at most the exact same as ChatGPT. That means that in principle, there's only going to be a few models that the vast majority of people will ever use. People can theoretically switch from model to model, but people tend to settle in with a product and develop brand loyalty. For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used. This partially offsets the risk of losing customers to a different product. Another way that companies can make money without having a moat is through institutional lock-in. Once a large corporation has integrated a particular AI into their day to day operation, transitioning away isn't costless. They may even have contracts agreeing to buy a certain amount of tokens, which binds them to keep using the AI instead of transitioning.
There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise
A potential way for a bubble to pop is for the companies involved to run out of capital to spend while they grow, causing them to fail. With the enormous amount of churn and debt that AI companies have, this is a serious risk to consider. Even so, I think that it's premature to worry about these companies failing to raise capital when most of them haven't even had an IPO yet. When SpaceX (which is partially an AI company, despite the name) went public, they raised more than 80 billion dollars. Besides that, many AI companies haven't issued public debt yet, which is a major way to get loans if private lenders decide that they don't want to put more of their capital into AI. The ones that have issued public debt, like Alphabet and Meta, have excellent bond ratings. If they need more capital, they won't struggle to find people to give them a loan.
Of course, investors aren't the only way to get capital. Once AI companies become profitable (as they already seem to be), they can use those profits to fund growth and pay off debts. The idea that AI companies are forced to constantly look for new investors to keep their doors open is probably a few months antiquated. From how it looks from Anthropic's S-1, the AI world may be past the horizon when it came to taking risky bets and can now focus on reaping the rewards.
The AI Industry Doesn't Look Like Any Bubble We've Seen Before
When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations, which makes the burst obvious in hindsight. With public AI companies, we don't see that happening. Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years, but all of them have stable P/E ratios in their 20s. If the increase in their valuations were irrational (or even just in expectation of future growth as opposed to current earnings), you would expect the P/E ratios to go up. Instead, their valuations look exactly what we would expect from a healthy trillion dollar company. When the dot-com bubble happened, it was largely driven by companies that couldn't turn a profit or had P/E ratios in the hundreds. I'm not going to pretend that I'm an expert on financial bubbles, but I've never heard of a bubble where the companies involved had such a modest valuation based on their earnings, even if their earnings (and therefore their evaluations) are enormous.
A potential way that this could be a bubble is if AI proves to be a fad. A lot of this rise in valuations has been because of increased demand for GPUs and data centre utilization, which is downstream of the demand for AI. We might imagine that the AI labs are propped up by an enormous amount of invested capital, and this capital ends up propping up the valuations for companies that make or rent out GPUs. However, this doesn't seem to be happening. Alphabet has a full-stack AI supply chain, where they create ASICs for AI, train their own AI, integrate AI into their products, and rent out compute to customers. Their prospectus helpfully divides their revenue streams into Google Cloud for their rented compute and Google Services, which makes it easy to tell if Alphabet's increased earnings are mostly because of their data centres. The answer is no. Google Cloud revenue is growing more in terms of percentage, but Google Services is growing far more in absolute terms. Specifically, Google Services revenue grew by 37.8 billion dollars for a 12% increase, while Google Cloud revenue grew by 15.5 billion dollars for a 36% increase. Alphabet is definitely benefiting from renting out their data centres, but it's not the main reason why their earnings have skyrocketed. Meta doesn't rent out their data centres at all, but their prospectus also records them having massive increases in their revenue, on the order of an extra 30 billion dollars from 2024 to 2025, and another extra 30 billion from 2023 to 2024. This isn't foolhardy investors throwing money at any company that makes AI, this is real profit from companies that have found ways to monetize AI. Anthropic also seems to be experiencing an exponential growth in their revenue as well, based on their S-1 filing. The only real unknown is OpenAI, which purchases an enormous amount of compute from other companies. It's possible that their finances are terrible, but even if they go under, I'm not convinced that this amounts to a bubble bursting. If anything, it seems more likely that their competitors will just consolidate and fight for more of a market share instead of the collapse triggering a chain reaction that takes the industry down with it.
Conclusion
I didn't write this article as some big takedown of the AI bubble theory. Even with this evidence, there are serious risks to the financial sustainability of the AI industry. Public backlash against data centres are going to make it harder for the infrastructure necessary for the AI revolution to continue, and regulatory barriers may make it harder to develop or deploy new models. Besides that, there's an enormous risk of an autonomous AI hacker causing serious damage, causing public demand for AI to plummet. Also, even after writing out it's possible for AI companies to pay off their debt, I'm still concerned by how much it actually is. It's not good that they're using increasingly complex ways to fund their infrastructure investments, and this gamble can backfire if revenue growth suddenly slows down, which it certainly might. Don't YOLO your life savings on the AI revolution, or at least don't blame me if you lose the shirt off of your back. The reason I wrote this article is because I felt that discussion about AI has become something of an echo chamber, which is never a good way to figure out what's right or wrong. Despite the echo chamber, people's stated beliefs and actual behaviour are wildly divergent. It's one thing to say that AI is a bubble that's going to burst, but where is this investor money coming from if we're all in agreement here? At the end of the day, when people have to put their money where their mouth is, they pull it out of their mouth and use it to buy NVIDIA. They might be wrong to do so, but maybe they're not. Time will tell.
As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be. People are afraid of what's going to happen with AI, and rightfully so. Beyond fear for the future, AI in the present has become uncomfortably common, with AI slop everywhere online and increasingly even IRL. This has all happened so fast, it's easy to forget that ChatGPT came out a little less than 4 years ago. Our world has changed in such a scary and odd way, and while I have a pretty optimistic view of AI overall, I get why people would want it all to go away. So, people wishcast. articles.title: Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
articles.body:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
·4 minute read
Today, we're introducing Muse Ember, our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.
Muse Ember delivers more intelligence per dollar than Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna at any reasoning setting: it matches Haiku's best score at about a third of the cost and beats every Luna setting. It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.
For more details about our evaluations, see our report.
Muse Ember is available today on the Meta Model API, at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens.
In early testing, our partners put Muse Ember to work on the kinds of tasks agents repeat all day, from reviewing contracts to writing code.
Agents
Agents spend most of their tokens on many small, structured steps, and Muse Ember is built for exactly that. It can carry a business workflow end to end, pulling records, calling tools in sequence, and updating systems across apps.
With a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens, it can take in a full codebase or document set in a single call.
Coding
Muse Ember is built for the coding subtasks an agent sends off hundreds of times a session: reading files, running tests, making targeted fixes.
For the hardest problems, pair it with Muse Wonder: Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.
Multimodal
Muse Ember natively understands text, images, audio, and video, so agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model. It can work through long real-world documents, operate a computer directly from screenshots, and pick out fine visual detail.
Safety
Before release, we evaluated Muse Ember under our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework, including chemical and biological, cybersecurity, and loss-of-control risks. Across the categories assessed, our evaluations found that Muse Ember remained below the framework’s high-risk thresholds. Though it’s a small model, it received the same core safety training and testing. We also evaluated how Muse Ember behaves when acting on users' behalf. That covers whether it respects user intent, handles sensitive information appropriately, resists instructions hidden in web pages, documents, or tool outputs that try to redirect it, and seeks human input before high-impact actions.
Availability
Muse Ember is available today on Muse Code and Meta Model API as muse-ember-1.0. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 per million cached input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1M-token context window and up to 512K output tokens. Muse Ember supports the Responses API.
When we introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, we said we would use them to develop specialized models we can bring to everyone. Muse Ember is the first trained using Muse Wonder Full. It rounds out our portfolio of models: Muse Wonder for the hardest problems, Muse Spark for coding and agentic workflows, and Muse Ember for repeatable coding and agentic tasks at scale at about $0.14 per Artificial Analysis task, a cost low enough to run in every product, for everyone.
Our goal is personal superintelligence: models that help you pursue your goals, create what you imagine, deepen your relationships, and take action on what you value most. Bringing it to everyone takes more than frontier capability. It takes frontier capability at a price that scales. We have even more efficient models in training and look forward to sharing what's next. Muse Ember, Muse Spark and Muse Wonder are now available on Google Cloud and Oracle Cloud.

articles.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
articles.body:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).
For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.
DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.
                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark.
Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE
It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch:
Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes
Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am)
Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable
Organization of connections into projects
Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.
Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.
The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.
Limitations:
It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon.
Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.
Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.
https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve

articles.title: E-means: 10x faster k-means at equal loss
articles.body:
I’m excited to open-source e-means: a modern, robust k-means algorithm developed at Meta FAIR. A replacement of Lloyd's algorithm, e-means delivers a ~10× speedup in both epochs and wall-clock time while achieving lower loss.
100,000 datapoints in 200 clusters, two wide Gaussians and three small ones, cut off at a box, on a light uniform background. Lloyd has 1 update against 97 per epoch for e-means.
Across a large range of scales and datasets, e-means reaches a test loss below Lloyd's at 25 epochs, in 1.2 to 3 epochs. Measured end to end, that is a 10–45× wall-clock reduction on GPU against the state-of-the-art Lloyd implementation (Flash-KMeans[2]), and 8–15× on CPU against Faiss[1]. Speed and quality usually trade against each other in k-means, while e-means achieves both better speed and loss.
Given a fixed dataset of n points X = {x1, ..., xn} ⊂ Rd and an integer k, the k-means problem is to find k centroids C = (c1, ..., ck) minimizing the mean squared distance between each point and its nearest centroid:
It's a static dataset, unlike codebook learning inside VQ-VAEs, where the distribution to cluster is constantly moving.
The goal of e-means is to provide a modern optimization rule for the k-means problem. We started this project from the following observations:
For e-means, we chose to do mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages[6], which we found to be most efficient for the k-means problem. Contrary to previous mini-batch approaches, e-means requires no hyperparameter tuning because it automatically sets the batch size and step size with scaling laws (see Automatic hyperparameter tuning with scaling laws). In addition, e-means improves the initialization and the dead-cluster revival strategy, adds a cosine-scheduled decay rate, and introduces a finalization stage that reduces the training loss for a negligible runtime penalty at the end of training. e-means is highly parallelizable, and comes with specialized kernels that translate its algorithmic advantage into wall-clock speedups.
The centroid update rule is the central component of e-means. This section aims to provide an overview of update rules for k-means clustering. All methods maintain, for each cluster j, a sum Sj and a count Nj of the points assigned to it, and take the centroid as their ratio:
They differ only in how Sj and Nj are updated. Below, sj and nj denote the sum and the count of the points in the current batch that are assigned to cluster j (both zero if none are).
Lloyd’s algorithm[7] assigns every point to its nearest centroid and recomputes the statistics from scratch, using the full dataset as the batch:
so cj is the exact mean of the points currently assigned to it. Each update costs one full pass over the data, and the procedure is repeated a fixed number of times (typically 20 to 50 iterations).
MacQueen’s update[3] accumulates the statistics without ever discarding them:
so cj is the uniform mean of every point assigned to cluster j since the start of training, including points assigned under earlier, possibly poor, centroid positions. This was later partially addressed by Staleness-Reduction Mini-Batch K-Means[8], a hybrid method between k-means and MacQueen. They obtained important speedups, but only on very low numbers of clusters.
e-means works on mini-batches and replaces this sum with an exponential moving average:
so older assignments are forgotten at rate α, and the centroid tracks recent assignments rather than the whole history. This update rule is typically used for moving distributions, hence their adoption for training VQ-VAEs[6]. What we found is that it’s also extremely efficient for static datasets if it’s combined with e-means’ other components, and hyperparameters are properly tuned.
The e-means project started from previous work at Meta FAIR by Hugo Touvron and Hervé Jégou, who had found that mini-batch k-means by gradient descent could beat Lloyd’s algorithm. While I could reproduce these results, I found that the performance of gradient-descent based centroid updates is unstable at large learning rates, unlike exponential moving average updates. I suspect that is because EMA updates guarantee that the centroid is always in the convex hull of points assigned to it, while gradient descent updates may overshoot past that hull.
In order to achieve the lowest loss at a fixed number of epochs, we chose exponential moving average updates, hence the name e-means for our method.
If you set the batch to the full dataset, B = n, and α = 1, then Nj and Sj become exactly the count and sum of the whole cluster, so one e-means iteration becomes exactly one Lloyd iteration. Lloyd is an extreme case of e-means without cosine scheduling on the learning rate. However, our hyperparameter search found that this extreme setting is highly suboptimal, which explains why e-means largely outperforms Lloyd. Below, the loss is measured for every batch size B and step α: Lloyd lands in a corner, well outside the region where the loss is lowest.
This hyperparameter study motivated us to derive scaling laws that automatically pick the optimal batch size B and step size α.
To better understand why e-means reaches better losses than Lloyd at convergence, we plotted a few trainings on toy datasets to evaluate their ability to escape local minima. Repeating trainings over 200 seeds, we found that e-means is much less likely to fall in pathological configurations compared to Lloyd.
Our explanation for that is that mini-batches provide more noisy updates that are more likely to explore the optimization landscape and escape local minima. Lloyd, with its always decreasing loss, is more likely to exploit found local minima and never escape them.
An essential property of e-means is that practitioners don't need to set any additional hyperparameter compared to Lloyd's algorithm. We fitted two scaling laws to set the batch size B and step size α0 from any problem's characteristics (n, k, T), and found them to exhibit strong generalization on unseen datasets and problem scales.
Regret = (MSE with the law − best MSE over the grid) / best MSE, median over configurations. Held-out datasets: SIFT, SPACEV, and the VIBE[9] datasets arXiv and AG-News. Held-out size: one value of n left out of the fit and predicted.
We propose two equations to choose the batch, the default law and the quality law. The “quality law” trades off throughput for better clustering quality against the “default” law. Below we plot the training data for our scaling laws: validation MSE against step size α0 (left) and batch size B (right).
Toy example showing the importance of dead-cluster revival.
The main issue with mini-batch k-means is that it is prone to “dead” clusters, centroids that end up with zero assigned points during optimization. This reduces the effective size of the codebook, which is especially problematic for the large codebooks increasingly used today.
A common mitigation is to reinitialize clusters that fall below a certain size threshold, as done in EnCodec[10], where dead centroids are simply replaced by random samples drawn from the incoming batch. While this helps, it does not fully resolve the issue. Instead of sampling arbitrary points from the batch, we revive dead clusters by splitting large, existing ones: we sample an active cluster with probability proportional to its size and split it into two. We found this approach, adapted from Faiss k-means, to be significantly more effective at eliminating dead clusters and preserving codebook capacity.
1 million vectors, k = 16,384, 5 epochs, mean over 5 seeds; only the revival policy varies. A cluster counts as dead when fewer than ten vectors are assigned to it at the end, a thousandth of an average cluster. Imbalance: how uneven the cluster sizes are (1 = all equal). From the paper’s revival ablation table.
We validated e-means on 24 different embedding and synthetic datasets and configurations (see paper). For the video we ran 234 configurations of e-means against k-means (16 datasets, 100k to 100M points): explore every curve in the results map.
Repo: faiss/contrib/e_means.

articles.title: Crypto foundation demanded employees endorse suicide pledge
articles.body:
On a Friday in March, employees at an international technology foundation received a 38-page document outlining leadership’s vision for the foundation for the next 1,000 years.
The document went out to all employees of The Ethereum Foundation, a nonprofit organization registered in Switzerland that supports Ethereum, a popular cryptocurrency platform and the second-largest blockchain network in the world, valued at about $300 billion, according to a federal lawsuit filed by a Boulder resident Wednesday in U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.
Titled “The Ethereum Foundation Mandate,” the document featured ethereal illustrated scenes of glowing lights and anime-style characters voyaging through dark forests. The pages featured white text against a navy blue background and were adorned with cartoon flowers, rainbows and diamonds.
And on page 11 — nestled between a winking anime woman and three yellow cats — was a suicide pledge.
Authors, maintainers, editors and distributors of “this software” would pledge to ensure the software remained free and publicly accessible, and would also vow to “take his or her own life with a sword upon failure to uphold any of the pledges in this license,” the illustration read. It was labeled “Source Seppuku License,” an apparent reference to a traditional Japanese ritual suicide.
When the document went out on that Friday in March, employees were told to commit to the principles in the mandate by Monday or quit their jobs, according to the lawsuit brought by Kayleen Fulton, a Boulder woman who was fired from the Ethereum Foundation after she led employee resistance to the suicide pledge.
Employees were to return a form with one of two options checked, according to a copy of the document included in legal filings.
Choice one: “I personally commit to the direction set out in the mandate, I commit to help translate it into thoroughly reasoned strategies for my domain, and I commit to an exclusive and energetic focus on the mission-critical tasks necessary for its implementation. From today and until my last day at the EF.”
Or choice two: “I cannot confidently commit to the above and would like to request my extra months of compensation and leave the EF without undue delay.”
An email to the foundation seeking comment on this story was not immediately returned Thursday, but a foundation leader at the time told employees the suicide pledge was not meant to be taken literally, according to the lawsuit. After employee pushback, managers updated the commitment form to clarify that the form had “nothing to do with literal seppuku,” according to the lawsuit.
Resistance to the suicide pledge was swift and vocal, and began when the Ethereum Foundation’s board put out a draft of the mandate to staff in late February, Fulton alleged in the lawsuit. Employees soon asked whether they were pledging to die by suicide and wondered in workplace forums whether the pledge was a test of their loyalty to Ethereum’s core principles. One employee referenced a colleague’s recent death by suicide.
“I have a new hire joining tomorrow,” another employee wrote in a discussion about the suicide pledge, according to the lawsuit. “The first thing he’s going to see… is a motion to drop a clause that mandates employees commit the ultimate sacrifice by falling on a sword.”
Nearly 80 of the foundation’s 250 or so employees voted to nix the suicide pledge after the draft was released, according to the lawsuit, but leadership at the Ethereum Foundation ignored their objections and included the pledge word-for-word in the final version of the mandate. The final published version presented the suicide pledge in an illustration instead of including it in the main body of the mandate, as it had been in the draft version.
The mandate’s visual aesthetic — the anime and other illustrations — reflected imagery from a controversial online figure who was known to promote “white nationalist ideology and disturbing pro-anorexia content,” according to the lawsuit.
When an Ethereum Foundation board member objected to the aesthetic, Ethereum founder Vitalik Buterin responded that “the controversialness (sic) of those aesthetics is itself part of the point,” according to the lawsuit.
After demanding that employees agree to the mandate, Bastian Aue, co-executive director of the Ethereum Foundation, defended the suicide pledge to employees as “part of the artwork of the mandate.”
It was, he said, “a cultural reference like other elements in there. Chosen deliberately, but not meant to be taken literally.”
In the days after the mandate was pushed out to employees, Fulton and a colleague organized and sent the foundation’s board a letter in which 53 employees endorsed the mandate’s general direction but declined to return the commitment form. The employees also declined to resign, according to the lawsuit.
Aue ultimately allowed the letter-signers to keep their jobs. But he fired Fulton and her colleague who helped organize the letter. Buterin later told Fulton — who had just been diagnosed with cancer — that the firing was about company dynamics, according to the lawsuit.
“If you reward making a stink with outcomes, then everyone will know that essentially making that kind of show both internally and externally is the way to cause outcomes inside of the EF,” he said, according to the lawsuit, which cited a recorded conversation between the pair.
The mandate started an exodus at the Ethereum Foundation, according to the lawsuit. The board member who’d objected to the mandate’s visual aesthetics started a sabbatical the day Fulton was fired and resigned in June. By September, eight senior employees had left, according to the lawsuit, and most of the 53 people who signed the letter had resigned or been terminated.
Fulton, who had earned a salary of $195,000 in her role at the Ethereum Foundation, sued for disability discrimination, retaliation, interference with her rights under the Family and Medical Leave Act, unfair employment practices and related claims. Her lawsuit notes that the Ethereum Foundation “does not hire or pay its United States staff in its own name,” but instead uses employer-of-record service companies.
One of her attorneys, James Bartolomei, declined to comment Thursday, saying the lawsuit spoke for itself.

articles.title: Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
articles.body:
Computer Science > Computation and Language
  [Submitted on 9 Oct 2026]
Title:Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
